exit code 0run at this build by the suite's own runner, in the snapshot of Zayn

72 passed and five were skipped. The skipped ones are the fixtures of level 3, and a skip is not a failure: a verifier that reads the file alone has nothing with which to decide who an actor is. It states its level, and the suite holds it to that level.

A verifier written by other hands is judged the same way. It claims a level, it is run on each fixture at or below that level, and the set of codes it reports is compared with the manifest's. The manifest gives each fixture its file, its level, the codes it must get and, at level 3, its symbol table.

Of the 77 fixtures, 28 must get no finding, and 23 of those are lawful twins of a fixture that gets a finding. And three kinds of finding have no fixture at all, each with its reason written in the manifest. One is the finding of level 4, which is a fact about a painted page. The other two are failures to parse: what a parser reports after its first failure differs from one parser to the next, and a fixture would bind every verifier to one parser's habits.

The suite holds no fixture above level 3, so its last line at level 4 says what a run at level 3 says. Level 4 needs a painted page, and chapter 10 measures one.

Two verifiers, one answer

The verifier that ran every page of this book is written in JavaScript. It is the reference.

The verifier a team installs is the zayn command, one file, written in another language. It is a port of the reference: the same verifier, written again. Its bar is set above the suite's. The suite compares codes. A gate is a check that must pass before a release, and the gate between the command and the reference compares every byte: what each prints, what each prints on failure, and the exit code, on every fixture and on a corpus, a large set of inputs that a program makes from the fixtures. The first lines of the gate's file state its rule: "There are NO allowed differences."

Why bytes, when the suite asks only for codes? The design of the command answers: a port that agrees on the codes and differs in a message "has changed what a person reads".

I asked for that command in these words, which the design keeps as I typed them: "We should not depend on Node or any other thing!" Node is the program that runs JavaScript.

The release notes record the runs. Those of release 0.1.0 record the gate's full run with no difference to the byte. Those of release 0.2.0 record the Windows file passing the suite, 77 fixtures of 77, and list the Linux and macOS files as built.

The same core is also compiled for the browser, 134584 bytes, so that a page can check a declaration with nothing installed. A proof page runs every fixture at every level through it and compares each answer with the command's: the record it compares with holds 308 answers for 77 fixtures.

The first lines of the gate's file also say what it proves, and I keep the sentence beside the result: "Parity is sameness, not rightness". A command that agrees with the reference on every input carries every mistake of the reference.

A third evaluator, and its differences

Two verifiers that share a design can share a blind spot. So the language itself was also written down a second time, in Haro, the language of this series' first book, which is a language for declaring languages. The declaration was written from the contract's data and the tables of the declarations. An evaluator is forged from that declaration, which means that a program makes it from the declaration with no hand in between, and it shares no code with the verifier.

It does not agree everywhere, and that is its use. A script compares the two. It ran the forged evaluator against the reference on 73 fixtures. The list of its differences holds 22 rows, four of them added on 8 November 2026 for the menu fixtures and written by expectation: from what the evaluator is expected to say, ahead of the run that confirms it. Each row names the fixture, what each of the two says, and the class of the difference. In nine rows both refuse and speak different codes. In three rows the forged evaluator refuses a file the verifier accepts. In 10 rows the verifier refuses or warns and the forged evaluator says clean, and the five fixtures of level 3 are among them. The script counts a fixture as agreed when the forged evaluator's first code is one of the codes expected: it speaks one refusal for a file, where the verifier reports them all. It also refuses the kinds of other languages, which the verifier passes over: the difference that chapter 7's exercise met.

The list is a ratchet, a list that may only shrink. The script fails when a difference appears that is not on it, when a listed row changes, and when a listed difference now agrees and is still listed. A difference can leave the list only by being repaired and removed.

Decisions on the record

What I refused

I refused to choose where the verifier lives before there was evidence. The decision document of 6 August 2026 sets the order: the fixtures and the specification first, before a verifier could pass them. Once a suite exists, two implementations that drift apart are a failing run.

I refused to fail a fixture that a verifier cannot see. A fixture above a verifier's level is skipped. A verifier that pretended to decide it would be claiming a level it does not have.

I refused a fixture for what a declaration cannot show. The finding of level 4 is a fact about a painted page. The manifest says of a fixture for it that it "would be theatre".

I refused a table that the verifier computes. A verifier that stands alone accepts the symbol table as an input. What the system around a declaration holds is that system's to say.

Where the field leads

The field leads in the number of hands. The web's suite is written to run in all browsers, and the results of an array of them are archived. Zayn's record holds one reference, one port of it in two builds, and one evaluator made another way, whose comparing script runs where the Haro forge is installed. The direction is the field's: more verifiers, written by other hands, each stating its level and listing its differences.

The field also has a third outcome beside passed and failed: inapplicable, the nearest thing to this suite's skip.

And a suite proves agreement. Whether what the verifiers agree on is right is the law's business, and Part VII's.

Part V · Chapter 12

One declaration, ten channels

Draft

Run on 2026-11-25 01:39 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 15 of 15 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other. In an exercise those lines are kept off the page, and the answer is folded until you open it.

A medium is the way an interface meets its user: a screen, a sound, a voice, a printed page, a lamp, a program that reads it. The Zayn site, and this chapter's title, call it a channel; this page says medium. In this chapter I write one declaration once, with no medium named, and check it on several media. Each medium is a row of data; the verifier holds the same row, checked against the data by the suite, and refuses what the medium cannot carry.

If you open the book here, four words are enough to follow. A declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface, the part of an interface that a user meets. The law is Zayn's constitution of 123 rules for interfaces. The verifier is the program that checks a declaration against the law. A verb is one of the law's 22 words for what a user does. The law's verbs, by family: DISCOVER, UNDERSTAND, LOCATE; FOCUS, FILTER, COMPARE; READ, SCAN, SCROLL, ZOOM; SELECT, HIGHLIGHT, PREVIEW, MARK; ACT, CONFIRM, CANCEL, UNDO; PAUSE, RESUME, RETRY, EXIT.

The field

The field adapts one document to several media. The W3C's Media Queries let an author write one stylesheet per medium: print "Matches printers, and devices intended to reproduce a printed display", and screen "Matches all devices that aren't matched by print." The specification also keeps a list of media types it has retired, speech among them, which a browser "must make … match nothing".

And the field asks that instructions and meaning never rest on one sensory characteristic alone. The accessibility guidelines say that instructions "do not rely solely on sensory characteristics of components such as shape, color, size, visual location, orientation, or sound", and that colour "is not used as the only visual means of conveying information".

Each source was read on 23 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them. So the field styles one document for each medium, and guards each meaning against a single sense.

The principle

A declaration says what a user does, whatever the medium; the medium a file names decides which of those promises can be kept, and the verifier refuses those that the medium cannot keep at all.

The contract, the file that binds each kind of finding to the law, gives the rule behind it in one sentence: "A new medium adds renderings, never verbs." The verbs stay the same on every medium, and each medium says which of them it can carry.

The media, as data

Each medium is a row of Zayn's data of the media. Six properties describe it: how long what it shows lasts, whether it shows things one after another or all at once, whether the user chose to look at it, how much it can carry at a time, whether it can change, and whether it can take back what it showed. And for each of the law's verbs, the row says whether the medium carries it fully, carries it at a cost, or does not carry it at all. The data defines the cost: "served, but at a cost the designer must know -- a parallel act becomes a serial one, or a perception becomes a memory task". The table counts, for each medium, the verbs in each of the three.

MediumWhat it isVerbs carried fully, at a cost, not at allMay carry a surface alone
visualA screen or page22 · 0 · 0yes
auditoryNon-speech sound15 · 6 · 1no
voiceSpeech in and out15 · 6 · 1yes
hapticTouch and vibration0 · 2 · 20no
printThe fixed record6 · 0 · 16yes
luminousIndicator light, lamp, beacon0 · 2 · 20no
signageFixed physical marking3 · 0 · 19yes
machineConsumed by a program22 · 0 · 0yes
spatialA world seen from a vantage22 · 0 · 0yes
terminalA text grid21 · 1 · 0yes

Printed from Zayn's data of the media (conformance/media.json): for each medium, how many of the law's verbs it carries, carries at a cost, or does not carry at all.

The last column is the data's column soleCarrier: a medium marked no should never carry a surface on its own. The data's note on sound gives the reason: "sound is the first thing switched off". Across the 10 rows there are 220 pairs of a medium and a verb, of which 126 are carried fully, 17 at a cost and 77 not at all.

The same declaration, three media

Here is a review of overdue invoices, written with no medium named.

Clean. An INTENT_FLOW is a flow: what a user does, from the first step to the last, to reach one goal. With no medium named, the declaration is checked by the law that holds on every medium. A VIBE is the kind of declaration that states a culture of interaction, and its field SURFACE_AS names the medium, the way the interface meets its user. Here is the same review, shown by a lamp.

Refused, once for each verb a lamp cannot carry: a lamp lets a user discover that something is wrong, and on it a user cannot go to an item, scan, compare or read. The declaration is the same; the medium decides. Here is the same review on a voice line.

Clean, though the data records that a voice carries scanning, going to an item and comparing at a cost. The cost is for the designer to read in the data, and it raises no finding. The data's own line on it: "Only 'absent' raises a diagnostic." Now two media in one file: a screen and the lamp beside it.

The same four refusals. Every medium that a file names applies to every declaration of the file, so the screen does not make up for the lamp.

A medium outside the list

The list of media is closed. Here is a lamp named in a word of its own.

Refused: the medium is outside the list. The data's name for a lamp is luminous, "Indicator light, lamp, beacon". Here is the same file with the data's word.

Named rightly, the lamp brings its own refusal: it cannot be read. The repair asks of a lamp what a lamp can do.

Clean.

A status that sounds like nothing

A medium also renders the statuses of a declaration: the words of SIGNALS for what a value says about its record, success, warning, danger, info and muted. To render one is to show it, sound it or say it. On a voice line, muted is rendered as silence. Here is a queue that a user hears, whose only status is that one.

Refused, under Rule 82, Article III and the right to know: every status the surface declares is rendered as nothing on this medium. The contract binds each kind of finding to its article: this one to Article III, the article Rule 82 derives from, and the refusals of a verb a medium cannot carry to Article II, the article of the verbs. A right is a sentence of the law about what the user is owed. Silence is the correct rendering of muted, and the contract says so: "silence is the CORRECT rendering of 'waiting, inactive'". The defect is a surface that has nothing else to say. The repair gives it a status that sounds.

Clean. The data records how three media render each status: the screen, sound and voice. The diagnostic reads those three; on another medium, a status passes it.

The machine medium

One medium is read by a program: machine, "Consumed by a program". Its user can be an AI agent. The data's note on it ties three beneficiaries together: "What a screen reader can operate, an agent can operate and a non-visual medium can render." Here is a batch that a program submits.

Refused: a flow that acts must keep cancel within reach, and the rule holds for a program as for a person. A single control, an INTERACTION, is held to its own promise instead. The repair keeps it there.

Clean. Part IX reads this medium at length, where the user is an AI agent.

Decisions on the record

What I refused

I made the medium a part of the law. In my pass of 13 August 2026 Rule 82 became Perceivable State: when the system knows something important, the user must be able to perceive it "in the medium the surface declares". The docket, the file where changes to the law are ruled, calls it "the load-bearing amendment of the medium axis." Every refusal of a medium on this page cites Rule 82.

I held the law of touch until a device gives evidence. In the same pass a rule whose title spoke of touch, haptic in the law's word, was renamed for what it governs, and the docket says that "the haptic law waits for device evidence".

I refused a promise the medium cannot keep. A promise of the way back on a printed page was once accepted, because the check read only what a declaration does and not what it keeps within reach. On 2 November 2026 I ruled that it was "silence hiding an error, so the verifier changes".

The data refuses a list made by taste. A medium enters it by its properties: "a new channel is classified rather than argued about." And the data names one word it kept out: "ambient is deliberately NOT a medium."

Where the field leads

The field leads on what is drawn: its standards for a medium come from surfaces that exist. In the data's words, Zayn's table of what each medium carries is "a first cut", "derived by reasoning about each medium's properties, not by rendering anything". So the field measures drawn surfaces, and Zayn reasons from properties.

In Zayn the cost of a medium is data for the designer and raises no finding, and the data marks the rows most likely to move: those of sound, voice and touch.

Zayn leads on refusing before the surface exists. A promise the declared medium cannot carry is refused in the declaration, on every medium the file names, with the rule that put the medium into the law.

Where it stands

The media are data at version 1.1 of their file. The verifier keeps its own copy of which medium carries which verb, and the suite checks that the copy matches the data before any fixture runs. Each plate of this page was run. Zayn's data records how the screen, sound and voice render each status, and their renderers are in a library of the estate. On a passing medium, such as a voice, whose words do not stay, a user keeps a right by being able to ask again, and the data calls a field to declare that a language change that "deserves its own decision".

Part V · Chapter 13

The grid

Draft

Run on 2026-11-25 01:39 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 10 of 10 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other. In an exercise those lines are kept off the page, and the answer is folded until you open it.

The grid is a map of what the law covers, drawn from what a user does with an interface. In this chapter I draw it: the media crossed with the activities of the user, the cells that no rule can hold, the cells that hold one and the cells that wait for one. I show how each rule finds its place. Then I run a rule on a cell where no rule is written, to see whether it answers there.

If you open the book here, four words are enough to follow, and an INTENT_FLOW, on the plates, is a flow: what a user does to reach one goal. A declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface. The law is Zayn's constitution of 123 rules for interfaces. The verifier is the program that checks a declaration against the law. A medium is the way an interface meets its user: a screen, a sound, a voice, a printed page, a program that reads it. The Zayn site and chapter 12 also call it a channel, and chapter 12 gives the 10 media of the law.

The field

The field has drawn maps of its rules. The accessibility guidelines are organised around "four principles", with their guidelines under them: one axis, the user's perception and use, with a tree beneath it.

The field has also separated what a user does from how it is drawn. W3C's Note on task models says that they "describe the logical activities that have to be carried out in order to reach the user's goals". Its Note on abstract interfaces describes an interface "independent of any interaction modality (e.g., graphical, vocal, haptic, 3D)".

Each source was read on 23 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them. So the field has a tree of principles, a model of the user's activities, and an interface held apart from its medium.

The principle

A cell holds a rule when a rule is written for it, so every empty cell shows where the law is projected today and where its next rule will stand.

To project a rule is to apply a rule that names no medium in one medium. The grid's page on the Zayn site says what an empty cell is: "an empty cell is a visible gap in the law, not a hidden one". The design document behind the page counts only the rules written for a cell, and gives the reason: a rule's projection into a cell is "a claim that the rule can be projected there". So the count shows what is written, and every empty cell stays in view.

Activities and media

The activities are what a user does: perceive, understand, decide, act, recover, trust. Each is a question the user asks of an interface, and none is named after a defect. The law's verbs, its words for what a user does, are shared among them, each verb once: understand owns the verbs of finding and reading; decide, those of choosing; act, ACT and CONFIRM; recover, those of the way back and of time. Perceive and trust own no verb, and the design document gives the reason for perceive: "Giving perceive the verb READ would have called a lit lamp unperceivable." So no medium is closed to perceiving or to trusting.

The media are the ten of the law, and one more, any: in the document's words, "the law stated without a medium, before it is projected into one". Here is the grid, counted from the data each time this book is built. It has a medium on each row and an activity in each column, as the site draws it. In the table, visual is the screen, auditory is sound that is not speech, voice is speech, and machine is a program that reads the interface.

The columns are the activities of the user: P perceive, U understand, D decide, A act, R recover, T trust. Counted at this build from the placement of the rules (doc/design/coverage-placement.json), the media (conformance/media.json) and the verbs each activity owns (doc/design/coverage-count.js). A number is the count of rules placed on the cell; closed means that the medium carries none of the verbs the activity owns.

Read the table by its kinds of cell. A closed cell is one that no rule can hold: the medium carries none of the verbs the activity owns. Every other cell is open. A number is the count of rules written for that activity in that medium, and a zero is an empty cell, where the next rule will stand. The grid has 66 cells: 11 are closed, and of the 55 open ones, 20 hold a rule and 35 are empty.

Two rows carry most of the law. Of the 121 rules placed, 94 sit on the screen, 26 name no medium, and Rule 125 sits on sound alone. A rule counts once in these figures, and once in each cell of the table where it is placed. The law is written for a screen, and the row any holds the rules stated for every medium.

How a rule finds its place

A rule's activities are read from its title and its reason. Its medium is found in three steps. First, a medium that its own words name. If none, no medium at all, when the kind of finding that enforces it ignores the medium, or when its text speaks of no screen. If neither, the screen. Rule 79, the undo rule, takes the second step: its finding is the same on every medium. Two rules are placed on no cell, and the file gives each a reason: one is a checklist applied to the other rules, and one concerns what a generator, a program that writes interfaces, ships.

The placement is a reading, and it was measured as one. On 3 November 2026 I ruled that it "be measured, not changed", and two readers, each of whom had not seen the placement, placed a sample of the rules again. They agreed on the medium more often than on the exact activities, and the design document draws the lesson: "The medium-free column is stable where a diagnostic is bound and soft where none is." The same day I ruled how a medium is named: "a rule sits on a medium only where its own words name it". The placements of Rules 60, 104, 123 and 125 changed.

A rule on an empty cell

The row any stands for every medium, so a rule that names no medium is projected onto the empty cells of its activity in every medium. Does it answer there? Here is Rule 79, which the placement puts on no medium, on a surface heard as sound.

Refused, under Rule 79, on a sound surface as on a screen. The declaration lands on recover by auditory, an empty cell, and the rule answers there. The lawful twin, the same declaration with the defect repaired, keeps undo within reach.

Clean. The rule fired on the defect and stayed quiet on its twin. Zayn has two verifiers: the reference that this page runs, and a second one built from another declaration of the language, which chapter 9 describes. When both agree on such a pair, the design document records that the rule "applies". Zayn's conformance suite, its set of fixtures, which are declarations kept with the answers they must get, holds such pairs for sound, voice, a program and print. Here is one more empty cell, recover by voice, measured on this page by a declaration of its own.

Refused. The lawful twin keeps undo within reach.

Clean. The run measured one more empty cell, and the grid's count stayed where it was, because the count is of the rules written for a cell, and this run wrote none. The design document says the same of the first projection fixtures: "No rule, diagnostic or verifier changed." The cell is measured, and it stays empty for its next rule.

A closed cell, refused

A closed cell is drawn on the grid, and the verifier refuses what lands there: it refuses each verb that a medium cannot carry, and on a closed cell none of the activity's verbs is carried. Print carries no verb of the way back. Here is a printed ledger that promises one.

A refusal for each promised verb that print cannot carry. Each cites Rule 82, the rule of perceivable state, which the contract's note says "is what made 'the declared medium' a legal concept". This kind of finding, VERB_NOT_CARRIED, once read only what a declaration satisfies, and a promise like this one passed. On 2 November 2026 I ruled that it was, in the design document's words, "silence hiding an error, so the verifier changes". The repair promises nothing that paper cannot keep.

Clean.

A rule satisfied on paper

A rule that names no medium can be satisfied in a medium where it has nothing to act on. Here is a printed notice that declares a motion.

Refused under Rule 112: motion that reports nothing is decoration. Now give the motion something to report.

Clean, and print has no time in which to fade. The design document records it as a gap of projection: "The rule is satisfied in a medium where it cannot apply". On 2 November 2026 the same ruling left it unchanged, because it hides no error. It stays, in the document's words, "open as a fact and closed as a question".

Decisions on the record

What I refused

I refused a rule written to fill an empty cell. My ruling of 2 November 2026, as the grid's document keeps it, "forbids writing a rule for them until that is measured": until the projection of the rules that already reach those cells is measured. The measurement came first, with the projection fixtures of this chapter.

I refused to change the placement when it was doubted. I ruled that it be measured instead, and then ruled how a medium is named.

The design document refused to count a projection as coverage. A rule that names no medium is projected onto every empty cell of its activity, and the count leaves those cells empty, so that each stays in view.

The design document keeps back rule text for haptic, luminous, signage, spatial and terminal, until a product that ships in one of them is named.

Where the field leads

The field leads on people. W3C's page on evaluation says that "Knowledgeable human evaluation is required to determine if a site is accessible." The grid's projection is measured by instrument, and the design document says so: the fixtures are "projected by instrument, not as verified by a person". A person's perception of each medium is next.

The field leads on the media themselves. What a medium carries is, in Zayn's data, "derived by reasoning about each medium's properties, not by rendering anything", and chapter 12 reads it.

Zayn leads on a map that is finite and counted. The verbs are a fixed list, and so are the media, so the grid has a fixed number of cells, a declaration that lands on a closed cell is refused, and an empty cell is printed on the public page with its count.

Where it stands

  • builtthe grid as data and as a page: 66 cells, 11 closed and 55 open, of which 20 hold a rule and 35 are empty, with 121 of the 123 rules placed; the projection fixtures, which apply a rule under a declared medium, run on this page; a declaration that lands on a closed cell refused by name
  • designedthe record by which a defect found in use lands on a cell
  • nextthe projection of the rules that name no medium into haptic, luminous, signage, spatial and terminal; rules written for those media once a product that ships in one is named; a person's perception of each medium

Built means that it ran on this page or runs in Zayn's repository at the release named under the title. Designed means that it is specified, and that its build comes after. Next names the direction.

The grid on this page is counted at each build from the placement of the rules, the media and the verbs each activity owns, and its figures equal those of the Zayn site. The projection fixtures show that rules which name no medium answer on sound, voice, a program and print as on a screen, and one projection on print is recorded as a gap of projection. The placement is a reading, measured by two readers and ruled on. Each of the 35 empty cells is projected onto by a rule that names no medium. A rule for each is for my ruling, after its projection is measured.

In your hands

This exercise is written for the book. Here an AI agent is the user: it orders stock through a supplier's interface for programs. A VIBE with SURFACE_AS machine says that the surface is read by a program. Write the finding you expect, by its code, then open the verifier's answer.

Now place it on the grid. The report cites Rule 16, and the grid's placement puts Rule 16 on decide, act and trust, with no medium named. The VIBE says the medium is a program. A declaration lands on the cells of the activities its findings' rules are placed on, in the medium its VIBE names. So this one lands on the row machine, in the columns D, A and T, decide, act and trust: look at the table, and each of those cells is empty. Repair the declaration. Try before you read on.

Clean. What is a confirmation when the user is an AI agent reading a surface made for programs? Zayn's data on the machine medium says: "What a screen reader can operate, an agent can operate". Whether that holds for a confirmation is the question that the next rule for decide, act or trust by machine will answer, and the grid keeps those cells empty for it.

A cell is a place where a rule can stand. Part VI asks who reads the interface that the rules describe: two cultures, under one law.

Part VII · Chapter 16

The constitution, part by part

Draft

Run on 2026-11-25 01:39 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 11 of 11 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other. In an exercise those lines are kept off the page, and the answer is folded until you open it.

The constitution of Zayn is one file. In this chapter I open that file and read it part by part: what it says of itself, its articles, its sets, one rule field by field, the rights of the user with the rules that enforce each, the patterns it forbids. On the way I make the verifier refuse four declarations, and I follow a citation back into the file.

If you open the book here, four words are enough to follow. A declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface: a screen, a voice, a printed page. The law is Zayn's constitution for interfaces. The verifier is the program that checks a declaration against the law. A finding is one entry of the verifier's report, and a refusal when it is an error.

The field

The field writes its rules as documents. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are organised around "four principles", with "a total of 13 guidelines", and their success criteria are numbered, like 3.3.4, and "written as testable criteria". A classic of the field is a list: the ten usability heuristics of Jakob Nielsen, which their page calls "broad rules of thumb".

For the people who test a page, the ACT Rules Format says what a test rule must state. Two of its parts are the applicability, "what parts of the test subject are tested", and the expectations, each of which is "an assertion about a test target".

And the field keeps some of its decisions as data. The Design Tokens format defines a token as information with "a human readable name": a colour, a dimension, a typeface. Those are values of the drawing.

So the field has documents, lists of advice, a format for a rule that a tester runs, and data for the values of a drawing. Each source was read on 21 or 23 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them.

The principle

The law is one file: the page that shows it is made from it, its counts are read from it, and a refusal that cites it uses its own numbers and names.

The file is named rules.json. It is written in a notation for data, names and values between braces. A designer reads the law in its reader, a page made from the file, and never in the notation. The verifier reads the same file at each run: the title of a rule and the numeral of an article in a report are looked up there. Every count of the law on this page is read from the file by the book's build, the program that makes these pages. Appendix A prints the law, set by set.

What the file says of itself

The file opens on its title, its version and its lineage, the dated list of its changes that chapter 18 reads. Then comes a preamble. It says what the law is for: "non-negotiable principles for business interfaces", which it wants "framework-agnostic, trend-resistant, and machine-checkable". In plain words: bound to no toolkit and to no fashion, and written so that a machine can check it. The preamble names its subject once: "the operator and the user name whoever acts through an interface: the user, a person or an agent". And it closes on short sentences, of which the last is "Undo is dignity." Article IV opens on the same words.

The word philosophy names two things in the file. One is a line of phrases, each of the form "X Over Y": calm over power, intent over mechanics, visible over hidden, business over technology. Four of the articles have one of them as their axiom, the phrase an article stands on. The other is a section of three principles, on the absence of pain, on empty space and on what lasts. The law's reader prints them before the articles, and they are outside the count of rules.

The articles

An article is a statement of principle, and every rule derives from one article. Each of the 123 rules names its article in a field, which is a name with its value: derived_from. Here are the articles, with the number of rules that derive from each.

ArticleIts keyIts titleIts sentenceRules derived from it
IcalmCalmThe interface must never compete with the operator’s thinking. Calm is a functional requirement, not an aesthetic choice — anything that draws attention without serving intent does not belong, whether it is drawn by a designer or spoken by a machine.34
IIintentIntent Over MechanicsInteraction starts from what the human is trying to do — discover, focus, read, select, act, recover — and widgets are consequences of intent, never primitives. Selection never implies execution; a flow that traps is unconstitutional.17
IIIvisibleVisible StateIf the system knows something important, the user must see it: active filters, pending drafts, norms, background work, and machine provenance alike. Invisible state is a violation.24
IVreversibilityReversibilityUndo is dignity. Every act is reversible, or explicitly and visibly irreversible — staged, named, and reviewed. Configuration never commits itself, and the way back is never broken.4
VauthorityPredictable AuthorityEvery consequential act names its actor, every claimed role is declared, and the same control always means the same thing. An intelligent agent is an actor under this law — never an authority above it.6
VIoperatorOperator Primacy and VibesBusiness users are operators, not explorers, and their culture deserves architectural respect: vibes, densities, dialects, and surfaces are equivalent vibes of one truth. Vibe-invariant rights never flex.37
VIIamendmentAmendmentThe law grows only from evidence: real usage, operator feedback, documented failure analysis. Removing a protection requires proof the harm is gone; adding one requires proof the harm is real and recurring. Trends, fashion, and developer convenience are not grounds. Retired numbers are never reused.1

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

The counts are uneven, and that is information. Most rules protect calm, visible state and the culture of an interface's users. Reversibility needs few rules, and the article on amendment fewest of all.

Read the last column. Why are a set's numbers not a range? Because a number is given once and never again, and a rule goes to the set of its subject. The rules are numbered up to 130 and the law holds 123: seven numbers are out of use, and the file lists them with what became of each.

One rule, field by field

Every rule has the same shape. Here is Rule 105, whole, as the file holds it.

Field, as the file names itWhat this rule holds
idthe-legibility-floor
number105
titleThe Legibility Floor
avoidBody text below 1rem; Muted grays that fail 4.5:1 contrast against their background; Accent-colored text that fails contrast on light backgrounds; Meaning conveyed by faintness
solutionMain reading text is at least 1rem with generous line height, and never lighter than 4.5:1 against its background; long-form prose aims for 7:1. Secondary text may be quieter in size or weight -- never in legibility. If a color carries meaning, it must also carry contrast.
whyText you must lean into is text you will misread -- faintness is not a design language, it is a tax on every reader.
derived_fromoperator
enforcementtool
invarianttrue

lintmeasured by tools/ui-audit.html: computed size and true contrast, every text node, both vibes

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

Every rule has nine fields. id is a handle, and number is what a citation names. title is printed after the number in a report. avoid is a list of defects and solution is the text of the rule: the list shows the rule broken, the text states it kept. why is the reason, in a sentence or two.

derived_from is the article, by its name in the file: here operator, which is Article VI. enforcement is the rule's tier: one of four words, here tool, and chapter 17 reads them. evidence says where the rule comes from. Rule 105's is printed as written, and the site it speaks of is the one that showed the law at the time.

Some rules have more: five other fields exist. invariant is a mark, the value true, on 47 rules. The law's reader prints it as the badge "vibe-invariant", and Article VI uses the same word of rights: "Vibe-invariant rights never flex." A vibe is a culture of interaction, and chapters 14 and 15 are about cultures. lint is a sentence that names a check or an instrument, the tool that makes a check, on 18 rules. vibes is a note for one culture or another, on 14. see_also points at a neighbouring rule, on seven. absorbs names the retired number that a rule took in, on five.

A right is what the user is owed, in one sentence, with the rules that enforce it. The file holds six; here they are.

A rule can stand in two lists: Rule 79 enforces the right to reverse and the right to act without fear. And a refusal can cite a right: eight of the 40 kinds of finding do. Here is a flow, which is a sequence of what a user does, that posts an entry to an accountant's ledger.

Refused! The report ends on the level, here 2: a run at level 2 makes every check that needs nothing but the file, those of level 1 included, and chapter 9 gives the four levels. It also ends on the exit code, the number the command returns: 1 for a refusal, 0 for a file that passes. Read the third line of the report: a rule, an article, a right. Now follow each into the file. Rule 79 is the rule whose number is 79. Its derived_from says reversibility, and that is the name of Article IV. No rule, article or right in the report's third line was typed into the verifier. The contract, which is the data file that binds each kind of finding to the law, says which rule, article and right this kind cites; the title and the numeral come from the law's file at the run. The repair is one word.

Clean. A second refusal, under another article and another right: a wizard, which is a flow with named steps.

Refused, and the citation names two rules: Rule 51 and Rule 53, both derived from Article II, and both in the list of the right to leave. One finding may cite several rules. The repair is again one word.

Clean. A third, under Article III and the right to know. A VIBE declares the culture of a surface and its medium, the channel through which it reaches its user. Here the medium is sound that is not speech: a queue monitor that a user hears. Its field SIGNALS lists the statuses that its values carry, from a closed list: success, warning, danger, info and muted.

Refused: Rule 82, Article III, the right to know. In sound, muted is rendered as silence, and that is right for muted. The defect is that it is the only status the monitor declares: its user hears nothing at all. The repair declares a status that sounds.

Clean. Three refusals, three articles, three rights, and each rule, article and right in a citation is a name or a number that the file holds.

Decisions on the record

What I refused

The law refuses a second use of a number. Article VII ends on it: "Retired numbers are never reused." Two numbers that an earlier numbering had given to what are now Rules 82 and 83 are marked in the file with these words: "Reserved, never to be assigned". Under Article VII, a citation of Rule 79 names the same rule in every version of the law, and the rule's evidence says what changed in it.

An amended rule keeps its number. When Rule 116 was first amended, on 5 August 2026, the lineage wrote: "No new number: the same rule, stated whole." A rule that changes is the same rule, with its history in its evidence.

No standard is cited before it is read. A proposal of August 2026 asked that a rule name the standards that support it, and set its own condition. In my pass of 13 August, a sitting where I ruled the proposals one by one, I accepted it as work to do. The docket, the file where changes to the law are proposed and ruled, keeps the condition: "nothing is written into rules.json" until the editions of those standards are read and their clauses recorded.

The law kept its role word. The law says operator where this book says user. On 7 November 2026 I answered yes to six recommendations of the docket, and one was that the law's prose name its subject as the user, a person or an AI agent. The word operator was left in the rules and in the title of Article VI, and the docket says why: "it is the law's role word, not a description of a human". Its remedy is one sentence of the preamble, which, in the docket's words, "makes every use of it mean the user, a person or an agent".

Where the field leads

The field leads on what stands behind a criterion. The criterion of the accessibility guidelines that chapter 8 read has a page of its own, which states its intent, and every criterion is "written as testable". Zayn's oldest rules share one line of evidence, and the rules that entered since version 2.1 each have their own.

Zayn's law leads on being read by tools. A count, a citation and a page all come from one file, so a rule's number means one thing wherever it is printed. The cost is beside the file: a text written by hand can differ from it, and Zayn's own ledger, the dated list of what the project found, says so in one line: "a number in prose is attached to nothing that can contradict it". This book takes the remedy that the same ledger gives: its counts of the law are read from the file at each build.

And the law's rules are equal in rank: when two speak of one subject they are reconciled, and chapter 18 tells one case.

Where it stands

  • builtthe law as one data file at version 3.17: a preamble, seven articles, six rights, 17 forbidden patterns and 31 sets of 123 rules; citations made of the file's numbers and names, run on this page; a reader that shows every part of the law, made from the file; the file identified by its hash in a pack of 12 files
  • designeda law in four layers: statute, core, commons and local; a field on a rule that records the sources which support it
  • nextthe law served to AI agents as they work, and rules moved to an instrument as each instrument is built

Built means that it ran on this page or runs in Zayn's repository at the release named under the title. Designed means that it is specified, and that its build comes after. Next names the direction.

Every table of this page was printed from the law's file at version 3.17, and each citation on it comes from a run. What reads the file at that version is the verifier, for the titles and the numerals of a report; the law's reader, for its parts; the Zayn site, for its figures; and the pack, the set of files that a user of the law keeps together, each identified by a fingerprint of its bytes. The law in four layers is a design: a statute above, a core that every interface keeps, a commons that teams add to, and a local layer of their own.

Part VII · Chapter 17Spine

The enforcement ladder

Draft

Run on 2026-11-25 01:40 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 14 of 14 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other. In an exercise those lines are kept off the page, and the answer is folded until you open it.

The enforcement ladder is the phrase the law's site uses for how its rules are held: each rule is filed under one word, its tier, which names the instrument the rule is owed. In this chapter I read those words. Then I set beside them what answers today: the verifier, which refuses a declaration; the audits, which measure a page; and a person, who judges. I show the verifier and the person at work on one surface, a help desk where an AI agent answers a customer, and the audits on their recorded runs. And I count which rules each instrument names, with the definition of the count printed beside every number.

If you open the book here, four words are enough to follow. A declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface. The law is Zayn's constitution of 123 rules for interfaces, kept as a data file. The verifier is the program that checks a declaration against the law. A finding is one entry of the verifier's report, and a refusal when it is an error.

The field

The field knows that its instruments reach part of a rule. The accessibility guidelines, WCAG, are published by W3C, the body that writes the web's standards. Their page on conformance says that the criteria are written "as testable criteria for objectively determining if content satisfies them", and adds that testing them "would involve a combination of automated testing and human evaluation". W3C's page on evaluation says it in one line: "no tool alone can determine if a site meets accessibility standards".

The tools say the same of themselves. axe-core, an engine that tests a page in a browser, says that with it "you can find on average 57% of WCAG issues automatically", a figure of its own, and that it returns an element as "incomplete" where "manual review is needed". A linter is a tool that checks source code against rules. One linter for the markup of a framework, the code that a browser draws a page from, says that it "only catches errors in static code", and sends its reader to a second tool for the page once it is drawn.

And the field gives each rule a severity. ESLint, a linter for code, lets its user set a rule to "warn", which "doesn't affect exit code", or to "error", whose "exit code is 1 when triggered". The exit code is the number a command returns when it ends, and a build, the program that assembles and checks a product, stops on 1.

Each source was read on 21 and 23 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them. So the field has instruments at two moments, before a page is drawn and after, a severity set rule by rule, and a person beside them.

The principle

A tier names the instrument a rule is owed; a citation shows the instrument that answers today.

The law's site calls the tiers a ladder: "Each rule declares one rung of an enforcement ladder, and rules climb as instruments are invented." A rung is a tier. The foot of the ladder is judgment, and the roadmap moves a rule up toward tool and machine as its instrument is built. A move up is a promotion, a change of the law that I rule. The docket, the file where changes to the law are ruled, says what a tier claims, in a sentence on Rule 127: it "is honest about which instrument owes the check; it is not a claim that the check runs today". A citation, the other half of the principle, is a rule named by number in what an instrument reports.

Decisions on the record

What I refused

I refused a tier that no instrument could serve. In my pass of 13 August 2026 a draft proposed to file Rule 62, on contrast, under machine. A declaration states no colours, so the verifier could never read it. I adopted the move to tool, an instrument that measures, and the docket keeps the reason: the draft "would have placed a rule in a tier no instrument could serve". Rule 38, on displacement, is filed under machine and answered by the audit: the filing and the instruments follow each other in part, and whether they should agree is a question filed for the law.

I deferred a requirement until it has evidence. A design note asked whether the law should require a role on every declaration that acts. On 19 August 2026 I ruled that requiring a role is, in the note's words, "deferred to evidence". A warning, ROLE_UNDECLARED, took its place: when no interaction of a file states a role, it tells whoever writes the declaration, and it refuses nothing. A run that holds only that warning ends with exit code 0.

The record refuses a count typed by hand. The ledger, the dated list of what the project found, has a line for counts like the ones on this page: "Counts and tier tables belong in code that reads rules.json". Every count of this chapter is computed at each build: from the law, the contract and the verifier's code, and for the audits from a list of citations that the build checks against each file.

Where the field leads

The field leads on its tools' account of themselves. An engine that tests a page in a browser publishes the share of issues it finds, and returns what it cannot decide as incomplete, for a person. The screenshot's checker in Zayn also gives an answer for what it cannot decide, and keeps a pass on size out of its own reach.

The field leads on severity. A linter's user sets each rule to warn or to error. In Zayn the contract fixes the severity of each kind of finding, the same for every team: a team gains one meaning of a refusal, and gives up a setting.

Zayn's law leads on saying, for every rule, which instrument it is owed, and on citing the rule by number in every finding of the verifier that binds a rule, and in most of the audit's. The ledger records where the verifier's reach ends, in a test of 12 August 2026: two payment surfaces "differing by seven broken laws" were the same declaration, byte for byte, and both ran clean. Its own words: "the court is silent exactly where the deterioration lives". The project answers with the audit of the painted page, and designs one more instrument: an audit that refuses at the moment of painting.

Part VII · Chapter 18

Amendment from evidence

Draft

Run on 2026-11-25 01:40 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 9 of 9 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other. In an exercise those lines are kept off the page, and the answer is folded until you open it.

An amendment is a change to what the law requires. In this chapter I tell how Zayn's law changes. I read its history in the file that holds it. I give three cases from the record: a remark on a screen that turned out to be law already, two rules that contradicted each other, and a check that ran before a rule was written for it. Then I list what moves when one rule moves.

If you open the book here, four words are enough to follow. A declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface. The law is Zayn's constitution of 123 rules for interfaces, kept as a data file. The verifier is the program that checks a declaration against the law. A finding is one entry of the verifier's report, and a refusal when it is an error.

The field

The field amends its standards by versions. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are at version 2.2, a W3C Recommendation. Its page lists the success criteria that are new in 2.2, and W3C's page on what is new says that the criteria of 2.0 and 2.1 are "essentially the same in 2.2, with one exception": criterion 4.1.1, which is "obsolete and removed". The standard prints the reason under the criterion's number: assistive technology "no longer has any need to directly parse HTML". The number stays on the page, with its note.

The W3C Process Document says how a Recommendation changes after it is published. It names a correction and an addition, and calls the two together "candidate amendments".

A regulation can then name one version. The fact sheet of the United States rule on the web content of state and local governments names "Version 2.1, Level AA" as its technical standard, with dates of compliance in April 2027 and April 2028.

A design system grows by criteria. The GOV.UK Design System asks of a proposal that there be evidence it would be "useful for many teams or services", and that it be unique. A linter, which is a tool that checks source code against rules, does the same for its rules: ESLint lists guidelines for a rule of its core, and says that since 2020 it accepts a new one only for a new feature of the language it checks.

And the field has a convention for what a version number promises. Semantic Versioning moves the first number when a change breaks what relied on the version before, the second for what is added, the third for a fix.

So the field amends by versions, admits by criteria, and keeps a removed number on its page. Each source was read on 23 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them.

The principle

The law changes only on evidence, and every change stays on the record: its date, its cause, and what it replaced.

The law says so itself, in its last article.

Article VIIAmendment

The law grows only from evidence: real usage, operator feedback, documented failure analysis. Removing a protection requires proof the harm is gone; adding one requires proof the harm is real and recurring. Trends, fashion, and developer convenience are not grounds. Retired numbers are never reused.

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

The article sets two burdens. To add a protection, the harm must be shown. To remove one, the harm must be shown to be gone. It names what is not a ground. And its last sentence is about numbers: a rule's number is a name, and a name that is given twice means two things.

The law's history, in its file

The law carries its history with it. The lineage is a list of dated entries, one for each state of the law: 32 entries, from version 2.0 on 3 August 2026 to version 3.17 on 12 November 2026. Most entries canonize a rule, which means that they give it a number and a place in a set. Some amend a rule and add none. Some are corrections of wording. Some change a word or a name.

What tells an amendment from a correction of wording? One question. The document that sets the law's architecture calls it the substance test: "does any interface that was lawful before become unlawful after — or must any conforming implementation change anything it does?" A conforming implementation is a tool that keeps to the law. If the answer is no, the change is a correction of wording, "however much prose changed". The first entry of 6 August 2026 is one: two lines of the law named a file that had moved, and no requirement moved with them.

The numbers have a history too. The rules are numbered up to 130 and the law holds 123, so seven numbers are out of use. Five are retired: each was a duplicate, folded into the rule that survives it, and the survivor says which number it absorbed. Two are reserved for good, because an earlier numbering had given them to what are now Rules 82 and 83. A number that is only proposed can be taken too. The docket is the file where changes to the law are proposed together and ruled item by item, in sittings that it calls passes. Rule 126 was first written under the number 125. The docket had already kept 125 for another candidate, so the new rule took 126. The docket's lesson: "a proposed number is not a free number".

Each of the 123 rules carries a field named evidence: what happened, where and when. Since version 3.13, an amended rule keeps its first evidence and gains a dated clause after it. The architecture document gives the rule for that field in four words: "Evidence is never corrected." What happened stays as it was written.

A remark that was already law

In August 2026 an AI agent that was not consulting the law built a status dashboard for me. I rejected two versions and corrected the third. The ledger is the dated list of what the project found, and it says what those corrections were worth: "Every correction he made was already law."

The first version was a grid of tiles, and the second was cards with coloured meters. My words, as the ledger keeps them: "use a classical table format not cards, it's more direct and less stressing to me". Rule 119 and Rule 94 already forbade both. Then came two red blocks, one under the other. Mine again: "having two red divs one under the other means we are not focusing on one critical thing." That was Rule 87. Then every table was wrapped in a container that scrolls sideways, which Rule 14 forbids. When that was removed, each row was stacked into a block, which is the first thing that Rule 95, a rule of the culture the law calls field, tells its reader to avoid.

So what did the episode add to the law? Five candidates were put to the docket on 15 August 2026. Two were refused as new law, because each was a rule that existed, and each of those rules was extended by a sentence. Three were canonized, and Rule 129 is one of them. The column that the scrollbar hid had carried my next action. The law forbade the scrollbar. It did not say "which column survives when width genuinely runs out", and that is the whole of the new rule.

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

Why is this evidence, and not compliance? Because the law stayed shut while it happened. The ledger's sentence names the law's file: "Nobody consulted rules.json while it happened". The docket gives the size of the case, "one surface, one operator, one implementer", and I print it at that size.

Two rules that contradicted each other

On 16 August 2026 Rule 3 and Rule 118 were put side by side: for the first time, by the ledger's account. Both speak of colour. Rule 3 kept the colour of danger for a failure of the system. Rule 118 gives danger to a value that is critical or exceeded. So a credit limit that is exceeded, coloured as danger, obeyed one rule and broke the other.

Which rule outranks the other? Neither: the ledger records that the law has "no precedence mechanism at all". I had delegated that pass to an AI agent, and the docket records it as a delegation. The pass invented no rule of precedence. On the colour of danger it gave the subject to Rule 118, "on the merits, not by seniority", and it amended both rules until they no longer overlapped: "Rule 3 owns chrome. Rule 118 owns what a colour means about a record." Chrome is the frame of an interface: its bars, its borders, its controls. Each rule now points at the other in a field named see_also, and seven rules carry such a pointer.

The language took Rule 118's statuses the same day, as the closed list of the field SIGNALS: success, warning, danger, info and muted. Here is a screen that uses two words of chrome as statuses.

Two refusals, and both cite Rule 118. The word danger passes. The other two belong to the frame, and the frame is Rule 3's. Here is Rule 118 as it stands after the amendment.

A check that became a rule

The usual order is a defect, then a rule, then a check. In one case the order was reversed. The verifier's check for an element that answers to no intent, whose code is INTENT_ORPHAN, had run since the first version of the language. Its findings cited Article II alone, with no numbered rule behind them. On 2 November 2026 Rule 130 was written for it, and the law went to version 3.12.

Here is a screen with one declaration, and its inventory: the list of the elements of the screen, which the verifier is given in a small file.

Refused. Read the third line of the report: it cites Rule 130. The record says that before version 3.12 the same file got the same refusal, citing the article alone, and the lineage sums up the amendment: "the refusal now cites a rule". No verdict moved. Rule 130's evidence says how it entered, and what it does not claim: "Canonized v3.12 from an existing check, which is the reverse of the usual order and is stated as such." Then: "No defect in a shipped interface is cited and none is claimed."

The repair gives the button a declaration.

Clean. The ruling of that day weighed two more of the kinds of finding that cite an article only, and left them so.

What moves with one rule

On 8 November 2026 I looked at a menu of the Zayn site and wrote a remark. Rule 116 was amended that day, and the law went to version 3.16. Chapter 19 follows that remark from my sentence to the check. Here is what moved.

The law's file moved first: the rule's text, then the version, the date and one more entry of the lineage. The language moved: fields entered it, so that a declaration can state a menu with levels. The contract moved: it is the data file that binds each kind of finding to the law it cites, and with the kinds that judge a menu it holds 40. The suite moved. The suite is Zayn's set of fixtures, and a fixture is a declaration kept with the answer it must get: one came for each new kind of finding, and one for a lawful menu, which makes 77. The Zayn site moved, because its menu is a declaration too, and the new kinds of finding judge it.

Then the pins moved. A pin is the version of the law that a file records as the one it was checked against.

A data file of ZaynThe version of the law it records

Read from each file at the version of Zayn this book reads.

At the version of Zayn this book reads, six data files carry a pin; counted at this build, six of them name version 3.17. A pin moves by a separate act, after the suite has run against the new law. The ledger tells what that act guards against. In August 2026 the suite's manifest, the file that lists the fixtures and their answers, was found pinned three versions behind the law it had passed against. It was found "by grepping for the field, not by any check": by a search through the files, made by hand.

A version is a name, and a name can be kept while the text under it changes. So each file that a team or a tool relies on also carries a hash. A hash is a fingerprint computed from a file's bytes. The pack is the set of 12 files that a user of the law pins, each with its hash, and its document sets the two side by side: "A version number says which edition you meant. A hash says the bytes you have are that edition." The version names; the hash proves.

One change in this chapter's record moved the language and left the law's version where it was. Chapter 7 showed it: a field on a kind of declaration that does not carry it has been refused since version 1.4 of the language, which numbers its versions apart from the law, and that finding cites Article II and no rule.

Decisions on the record

What I refused

I refused a sixth status. In my pass of 13 August 2026 a draft proposed to add a value to the statuses of Rule 118. The ruling adopted the proposal without the value: "the closed set stays at five". The data file of the vocabulary says what a sixth would be: "a constitutional amendment, not an implementation choice".

I refused a title that promised more than its rule. Rule 69's title promised a law for haptic feedback, the answer a device gives by touch, and its text governed touch targets and swipes. The same pass renamed the rule for what it governs. The docket's line is: "the haptic law waits for device evidence".

A rule waits for a second case. On 3 November 2026 a pass that I had delegated met a candidate rule: one subject, one page. It kept the candidate open, with these words: "The evidence is one author's reading of one site, not a measurement; it is not ratified now." Four days later another candidate, drawn from one site, was written up and kept as a candidate: "it would want a second site before a ruling". One case shows that a defect exists. Article VII asks that a harm be "real and recurring", and the docket states the size of every case it admits: Rule 129 rests on one surface, and its record says so.

The record refuses to be rewritten. The ledger opens on its rule: "Append, never rewrite." An entry that is later found false keeps its text and gains a correcting entry. One section of the ledger lists the corrections the project made to itself, and gives its reason: a project "that argues about drift and hides its own errors has refuted itself". Drift is a text that no longer matches the data it describes.

Where the field leads

The field leads on how many cases stand behind a rule. A design system asks for evidence from many teams. The W3C Process asks for wide review of a change, with the aim that the web community, "including the general public", has had notice of it. Several of Zayn's newest rules rest on one surface, and the docket says so of each. It also names the risk of a law that takes its rules one case at a time: "Three new numbers from one surface is a lot, and the risk is corpus inflation." A corpus is a body of recorded cases.

The field leads on procedure. The W3C Process is a document of its own, with its terms for a correction, an addition and a review. On Zayn's docket I rule alone, and the docket records each pass I delegated as a delegation.

Zayn's law leads on what it keeps of each change. Every rule carries its evidence, every change is a dated entry in the law's file, and a number is never given twice: the pack's document promises of one rule that it "means the same thing in ten years". And an amendment reaches the tools at once: on 16 August and on 8 November 2026 the language took an amendment on the day it was ruled.

Both sides know the cost of a pin. A regulation that names version 2.1 goes on naming it when the standard is at 2.2. A file pinned at one version of Zayn's law goes on reading that version, and the docket says of a user of the law that it "moves its pin deliberately". Zayn's law numbers its versions its own way: one of its first two numbers moves when its substance moves, the second from 3.1 to 3.17, and a third, as in 3.7.1, marks a correction of wording. So version 3.16, which added three refusals of a menu, is a step of the second number, where Semantic Versioning would ask for the first; a team that keeps its pin keeps the law it checked against.

Where it stands

  • builtArticle VII as data; a lineage of 32 dated entries inside the law's file; five retired and two reserved numbers; an evidence field on each of the 123 rules; the amendments of versions 3.11, 3.12 and 3.16 answered by the verifier on this page; six data files that record the version of the law they were checked against, and a pack of 12 files, each with its hash
  • designeda law in four layers: statute, core, commons and local; the test and the record by which a contributed rule is admitted
  • nextrules moved to an instrument as each instrument is built, and a law fed by the corrections of the people who use it

Built means that it ran on this page or runs in Zayn's repository at the release named under the title. Designed means that it is specified, and that its build comes after. Next names the direction.

The history told here is data of the law's file at version 3.17, and the amendments of versions 3.11, 3.12 and 3.16 were answered on this page by the verifier of release 0.2.0. What was lawful before a version is told from the record: this page runs one verifier, today's. Two rules that touch one subject are reconciled by amending both, and the pair is found by whoever puts them side by side; a rule of precedence, or a check for two rules on one subject, is a question that the docket has filed for me. The evidence behind a rule is of the size its field states: a body of recorded corrections for some, one surface for others, a decision or a check for two, and each rule says which. The law in four layers, with its commons, is a design: it is written, and it waits for my pass, section by section.

In your hands

Here is the menu that the Zayn site had from 6 to 8 November 2026, written small. A NAV_GRAPH is the kind of declaration that states an entry of a menu. LABEL is the name the menu shows, TARGET is the page the entry leads to, and ENTRIES lists its children in order. An entry with a target and children is a section, and the page it leads to is its landing page.

Write the code you expect, then open the verifier's answer. The section leads to a page that the level under it does not show. Put the page back under the section's name, and say what you expect.

Refused again, for the name. This is the defect my first remark named, in its plainest form: a reader meets the section's title, then finds it again among its entries. Chapter 19 gives that remark's own example. Give the page another label, and put it last.

Refused for the place. The report's first line counts it for you: entry 3 of 3. Repair it. Try before you read on.

Clean. Now go back to the first menu of this exercise, the one with its landing page absent, and delete one line: TARGET billing_home. Change nothing else, and say what you expect.

Clean. The specification of the language calls an entry with children and no target a bar, like the main menu, and a bar has no landing page. So the section passes once it stops saying where it leads. Should an entry that carries a label and leads nowhere be read as a bar? That is a remark for the law, and the law grows from remarks: this one is filed with the book's findings, for the next pass.

The usual order begins with a remark that someone wrote down. The next chapter follows one, field by field, from the sentence to the check.

Part VII · Chapter 19

How to write a rule

Draft

Run on 2026-11-25 01:40 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 12 of 12 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other. In an exercise those lines are kept off the page, and the answer is folded until you open it.

A rule is a remark that was kept. In this chapter I follow a remark of mine on a menu, and the second remark that its repair called for, from the sentences I typed to a rule with a check. There are seven steps. Each is shown on the record of those remarks, and a team can take the same steps for rules of its own. The chapter ends on a template that you can fill.

If you open the book here, four words are enough to follow. A declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface. The law is Zayn's constitution for interfaces. The verifier is the program that checks a declaration against the law. A finding is one entry of the verifier's report, and a refusal when it is an error.

The field

The field has written down what a rule must be, more than once. The page that explains conformance to the accessibility guidelines says that their criteria are "written as testable criteria". ACT, the format for the rules that testers run, asks that each expectation of a rule be "distinct, unambiguous, and be written in plain language". A document of the internet's engineers, a Best Current Practice of 1997, gives the word MUST one meaning, "an absolute requirement of the specification", and adds that such words "must be used with care and sparingly".

Those who keep a body of rules have criteria for a new one. ESLint is a linter, a tool that checks source code against rules. It asks a rule of its core to be atomic, "Rules must function completely on their own", and unique: "No two rules can produce the same warning." The GOV.UK Design System asks a proposed component or pattern to be useful, with evidence, and one that "does not replicate something already in the Design System".

Each source was read on 23 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them. Between them they ask four things of a rule: it can be tested, its words are exact, it stands alone, and it does not say again what is already said.

The principle

A remark becomes a rule when it names its cause, is bounded on both sides, and keeps the check that failed on the page as it was.

A bound is an edge of what the rule allows. The rule states the least and the most, so that a repair stops where it should. Zayn's design study, written from the corpus of its corrections, has the sentence this chapter stands on: "A correction stored as a symptom does not stop the defect; it moves it." The law has its own, in the reason of Rule 78: "A law that cannot be tested at the door will be negotiated in the hallway." A rule is tested at the door by its check.

Write the remark down

First, keep the remark as it was made. Zayn calls such a remark a correction, and keeps its corrections in a corpus: a data file of 489 records. Each record has the words, the page or the file where they were said, the date where it is known, what was wrong, what was asked, and what the remark concerned. 235 of them keep the person's words as typed.

Here is mine, of 6 November 2026, on the menu of the Zayn site: "the same menu option in the main and submenu levels (like Try and then Try here)!!!" A section named Try opened on an entry named Try here: the level under a section said the section's name again. The repair that followed deleted that entry, and with it the section's own page left the level under the section. On 8 November I wrote a second remark, and the corpus keeps its typing: "you must bring bakc the frist option but find an other lable for it".

One more field of a record matters here, and it is the one that makes a rule necessary: whether an earlier correction of the same defect exists. 174 of the 489 records say yes. My second remark is one of them, and its record says what the first repair broke.

Here is another section of that menu, Approach, as the second remark found it, written as a declaration. A NAV_GRAPH states an entry of a menu: LABEL is the name it shows, TARGET the page it leads to, ENTRIES its children in order. An entry with a target and children is a section, and the page it leads to is its landing page. You repaired a menu like it in chapter 18.

Refused: no entry under Approach leads to its page, and the report cites Rule 116. The declaration is written for this book from the sentence of the docket on that menu; the docket is the file where changes to the law are proposed and ruled. The check that answers it is the one the remark produced, and it fails on the page as it was.

Ask whether it is law already

The second step is a search: look for the rule that already covers the remark. In August 2026 five candidates for a rule came from one surface. Three became rules. Two were refused as new rules, because each was a rule that existed, and each of those rules gained the new case. The docket's sentence on one of the two: "The author's correction and Rule 113 are the same law, reached twice." The law was extended, and its count stayed.

A declaration can ask the question. The other of the two said that a status board must show what it requires of its user. Here is such a board, checked at level 3, where the verifier is given a list of what the system holds.

Refused, and the citation is the answer: Rule 82. The candidate has a number already. The repair is the board's, and the law stays as it is.

Clean. A search that finds nothing needs a control: a term that you know is in the law. Zayn's ledger, the dated list of what the project found, records a search of the law that returned nothing for every term, the word undo included, in a law that has a rule on undo. Its lesson is in the imperative: "Put a control in every corpus test". A search proves itself on a term it must find.

My remarks on the Zayn site went the same way. In November 2026 a table of them was filed in the docket under the heading "evidence for existing rules, not new rules", most beside the rule they support.

For the menu the answer was yes: Rule 116 has covered the subject since August 2026. So the remark became an amendment of that rule, and took no new number. Here is Rule 116 as amended.
