Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

Its last line is the reason: a menu hands its user a map.

Give it the law's shape

Third, write the rule in the shape that every rule has: what to avoid, as a list; the rule's text; its reason, in a sentence or two; the article, one of the law's statements of principle, that it derives from; and its evidence, which says where the rule comes from. Chapter 16 printed one rule whole. Three things make the rule hold: its cause, its two bounds and its evidence.

The cause. For the menu it was this: the entry of the main menu names a section, and the first entry under it names the section's landing page. The docket's words: "they are two things, so each keeps one name". A cause settles the next case, which a symptom leaves open.

The two bounds. My first remark had one: no repeated label. The repair went past it and deleted the page. The amended rule has both, and its list of what to avoid gained two entries: "A section whose landing page is missing from the level under it, or listed after the pages it leads to", and "A child entry that carries its parent's label, or two entries at one level that carry one label". Here is that first bound, still at work, on the same section.

Refused, on the other side. Here is the menu with the label that the site's writing rule records for that page, written here as a declaration.

Clean! Between the two refusals, the rule has its room.

The evidence. It is written as it happened. The document of the law's architecture has the sentence for it, "Evidence is never corrected.", and a rule that entered another way says so: the evidence of Rule 130 calls its origin "the reverse of the usual order". What happened is kept as it was told.

Name the instrument, then the tier

Fourth, ask clause by clause what can decide the rule. An instrument is what makes a check: the verifier, an audit of the painted page, or a person who reads. For Rule 116 the answer comes from three places. A declaration decides three of its demands, and you have just run two of them. The audit of chapter 10 reads the menu, the level under it, the trail and the outline as a browser paints them. And one clause stays with a person: the rule lists, to avoid, "A label that names the author's metaphor and not what the page holds". Here is a menu that the verifier passes and that clause refuses.

Clean, and wrong for a person who reads it: neither label says what its page holds. The verifier judges what a declaration states, and whether a word is a metaphor is a person's to say.

Then the tier. A rule's tier is one word in the law's file, and the card above shows Rule 116's. The docket says of one rule what that word claims: the tier "is honest about which instrument owes the check; it is not a claim that the check runs today". A rule can also point at its instrument, in a field of its own, and the pointer is written when the instrument exists: the docket left one out, because "a pointer to an instrument that does not exist is worse than silence". When Rule 116 gained its checks on a declaration, its tier stayed, and the docket left the question to me: "whether that moves the tier is a ruling, not this desk's". Chapter 17 reads the tiers.

Place it on the grid

Fifth, place the rule: which activity of the user it protects, and on which media. The grid crosses the activities of the user, perceive, understand, decide, act, recover and trust, with the media, and chapter 13 gives it whole. The placement reads the activity from the rule's title and its reason, and the medium from the rule's own words; a rule whose check does not look at the medium is placed on every medium. Does the menu's check look at the medium? Here is the defect of the repeated name on a surface that speaks. A VIBE declares the surface, here a voice, and the first choice under Orders is the same word without its capital.

Refused, on a voice surface as on a screen. The verifier compares whole labels, ignoring capitals, the spaces around a label and a leading The, for each of its three checks of a menu. The repair is the same.

Clean. In the grid's data, Rule 116 is placed on the visual medium, under the activity of understanding. The run says that this check answers on a voice surface as on a screen. So an amended rule is to be placed again, and that is one more thing an amendment touches.

Write the check that fails first

Sixth, write the check so that it fails on the page as it was and passes on the page as corrected, with one repair between the two and nothing else changed. That is what keeps the defect it was written for from coming back. The first plate of this chapter and the last plate of the third step are that pair.

Zayn's suite has it as a discipline for its fixtures, the declarations it keeps with the answers they must get: "One fixture, one concern", and for every refused fixture "a lawful twin where the defect is repaired and nothing else changes". The suite's guide gives the twin its reason: it "proves the check is not simply firing on everything". The suite compares the set of codes that a verifier reports, and nothing else: the subject, the line and the number of times a code appears are free. The amendment of Rule 116 brought one fixture for each new kind of finding, and one lawful menu from which each differs by a line. Where only a painted page can decide, the suite keeps no fixture and says why: "A fixture here would be theatre".

The same discipline applies where a check reads files or a painted page. The design study records its checks on the site's files "each shown failing on the pages as they were first", and of one more file check, which reads that a statement is made once on a screen, it gives the count: "35 of the 39 pages failed it". It also records what happens to a check written as a list of the kinds of element it covers: "the defect came back that afternoon on a kind not in the list". A check reads every element. And a check proves itself on the day it fails on the defect it was written for.

Amend what it touches

Seventh, list what the rule touches, object by object, and change each. Chapter 18 listed them for this remark: the rule's fields, the version and its line of history, the language, the contract, the fixtures, the pins. One more is the nearest: the pages of those who apply the rule. At the version this book reads, the site's menu keeps the page Reasoning in another section, Why, which opens on its own page. Here is that section, with its family entry left out, to show the rule kept on the site's own menu: the section opens on its own page, under a label of its own.

Clean. The remark went further than the site: the house that publishes this book adopted the same three kinds of finding for the menu of every book it puts online, this one included.

The template

Seven steps, and what each one writes.

StepWhat you write
1. The remarkThe person's sentence as typed; the page or the file; the date; what was wrong; what was asked; whether an earlier correction of the same defect exists, and what its repair broke
2. Already law?The rule that covers it, by number, and the case added to that rule; or how you searched, and the control that proved the search works
3. The ruleWhat to avoid, as a list; the text; the reason; the article; the evidence; the least and the most the rule allows
4. The instrumentWhich clause a declaration decides, which a painted page decides, which a person decides; the tier; a pointer when the instrument exists
5. The gridThe activity of the user it protects; the media its own words name, or every medium
6. The checkThe page as it was, and the finding expected; the page as corrected, with one change; a case the check must leave alone
7. What it touchesThe rule's fields; the version and its line of history; the rules it cites or narrows; the checks and their fixtures; the placement; the pages and the teams to tell

Row 6 asks one thing more than the plates showed: a case that the check must leave alone, so that it fails for its defect and for nothing else.

Decisions on the record

What I refused

I refused the repair made on my first remark. It had deleted the landing page from the level under its section. My ruling of 8 November 2026 brought the page back under another label, and the docket says of that ruling that it "reverses the reading of 2026-11-06". A remark with one bound had been read past its bound.

I refused a rule written to fill a cell. The grid of chapter 13 has cells that no rule names a medium for. My ruling, as the grid's document keeps it, "forbids writing a rule for them until that is measured". A rule answers a defect that happened; an empty cell is a question.

Where the field leads

The field leads on the form of a rule that a tester runs. The ACT format asks for a rule's applicability and its expectations, with examples that pass, fail and do not apply. A rule of Zayn's law has a list of what to avoid and a text, and the examples live apart from it, in the suite's fixtures.

The field leads on the words of obligation. The engineers' document says exactly what MUST means. Zayn's rules are written in sentences, and what binds in them is the check and its fixture where one exists, a person's judgment elsewhere.

Zayn's part is the path from a remark. A correction is kept with its words and its place; the rule keeps it as evidence; the check fails on the page as it was. The cost is stated too: a rule drawn from one case is as wide as that case, and one of the newest candidates is kept as a candidate until a second site is measured.

Part IX · Chapter 22Spine

The AI agent under the law

Draft

Run on 2026-11-25 01:41 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 13 of 13 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other. In an exercise those lines are kept off the page, and the answer is folded until you open it.

An AI agent under the law is an AI agent that the law counts as an actor: named in a declaration as a person who acts is named, and held to the same rules. In this chapter I read the law's article on authority and its set of rules for AI agents, rule by rule, each with its reason. I run declarations that show the verifier judging what a declaration states, whoever wrote it and whoever acts. I show the set's one check, on a proposal, where its reach ends, and what a person reads in its place. And I say how an AI model works with the law today, while it writes.

If you open the book here, six words come first, and every other word is said where it first appears. A declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface. The law is Zayn's constitution of 123 rules for interfaces, kept as a data file. Its rules are numbered to 130, because a number taken out of use is never given again. The verifier is the program that checks a declaration against the law. A finding is one entry of the verifier's report, and a refusal when it is an error. An AI model is a program that writes text, a declaration among others, from what it is asked. An AI agent is a program, driven by an AI model, that acts for a user.

The field

The field, the practice and the texts outside Zayn, governs the AI agent from three sides. The first side is guidance for design. Microsoft's Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction number eighteen, G1 to G18, among them "G8: Support efficient dismissal.", "G9: Support efficient correction.", "G11: Make clear why the system did what it did." and "G16: Convey the consequences of user actions."

The second side is statute. The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, asks that the people who talk with an AI system are "informed that they are interacting with an AI system" (Article 50(1)). It asks that what such systems generate is "marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated" (Article 50(2)). And for the systems it calls high-risk, it asks that a person can "disregard, override or reverse the output" (Article 14(4)(d)).

The third side is protocol, the rules by which programs talk while an AI agent works. The Model Context Protocol, MCP, connects an AI application, which it calls the host, to servers, programs that offer it data, prepared messages and tools, each tool "Functions for the AI model to execute". Its overview says that "Hosts must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool", that is, before calling it. A2UI, a format for interfaces that an AI agent composes, "Streams declarative JSON data with two-way bindings — never executable code": the AI agent sends a description of the interface as data, and the application draws it from parts it registered. "Agents place only components you registered."

Each source was read on 24 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them. So the field advises at design, binds by statute in use, and asks for consent while the AI agent works.

The principle

An AI agent acts under the same law as a person, and a declaration is judged by what it states, whoever wrote it.

The law says it in its fifth article, the one on authority.

Article VPredictable Authority

Every consequential act names its actor, every claimed role is declared, and the same control always means the same thing. An intelligent agent is an actor under this law — never an authority above it.

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

An actor is whoever performs an act. An authority above the law would be an actor whose acts the law does not judge. The set of rules written for AI agents opens on the same line, "an AI is an actor under the constitution, never an authority above it", and closes on what it asks, in three parts: "Same norms, same audit, same dignity."

Set 31, rule by rule

The law gathers its rules into sets, and Set 31, Intelligence Under Law, holds the rules written for AI agents. Rules 97 to 104 entered the law with its version 2.0, on 3 August 2026, and Rules 121 and 124 with version 3.7. Here they are, each with the reason it gives, the article it derives from, and its tier: the word under which the law files the rule, naming what is to check it. A proposal of the project for a new base of the law, its second founding, which awaits my ruling, glosses the two tiers of this set: judgment, "a human decides, until an instrument is invented", and machine-later, "the law's own admission that the instrument is missing". A tier names what a rule is owed; a check may read one clause of the rule before then, as PROPOSAL_COMMITS reads Rule 98's, and chapter 17 counts which. The last column gives the kinds of finding of the contract that cite the rule. The contract is the file that ties each kind of finding to the rules it cites, and a kind of finding is named by a code in capitals, such as MISSING_UNDO.

The rules of Set 31, Intelligence Under Law, with the reason each gives. Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

Read the reasons first: they are the law's own case for each rule. Each rule also gives a solution, which the table leaves out. Rule 97's makes the AI agent an actor, "named in the step, subject to the same validations, norms, signatures, and audit trail as any human". Rule 98's makes an AI model's output a proposal, which "becomes a commit only through an authority the declaration names". A commit is the act that changes what is true in the records. Rule 99's asks that what a machine wrote is marked as such, Rule 102's that a person is always reachable.

Then read the last column: what the verifier reads of the set is PROPOSAL_COMMITS, for Rule 98. Article V is cited as well by HIDDEN_AUTHORITY, for Rule 83: the check that, at level 3, asks every act to name its actor. A level is how much the verifier is given. The contract files each kind of finding at one of four levels: level 1 checks that the file is well formed and uses the language's own words, level 2 decides what a single declaration states, level 3 adds a table of what the system holds, and level 4 is the painted page, the page as a browser draws it. A run at a level reports the findings of the levels below it too. At level 3 the table lists the system's actors, and every declaration whose SATISFIES holds ACT must name an actor. Chapter 9 runs HIDDEN_AUTHORITY. Article V and Rule 83 bear the same title.

Whoever wrote it, whoever acts

Here is a reconciliation desk in accounts. An AI agent matches the lines of a bank statement to invoices, and an accountant answers for the books. Say an AI model wrote the first declaration of the desk, and left a comment on its first line, which the verifier skips. An INTENT_FLOW is a flow, what a user does to reach one goal: SATISFIES lists the verbs it carries out, ALWAYS_REACHABLE the verbs that stay within reach at every step, and ACTOR names who acts.

Refused, under Rule 79, the rule the comment says was kept: the act keeps no undo. The report ends on the exit code, the number the command returns: 1 when it refuses, 0 when it accepts. Now the same flow as a person would write it, for the accountant to apply.

The writer changed and the actor changed, and the report did not: the same refusal, the same rule, the same right, to reverse. The verifier reads the fields, never the writer, and holds the AI agent's act to Rule 79 as it holds the accountant's. The repair is one word for both.

Clean. A claim to have kept a rule is a comment, and the verifier's answer is the run.

A proposal and its authority

Rule 98 has a word in the language: the role proposal. A role is the promise a control makes about what happens when it is used. A control is an INTERACTION, and its role is one of these words: inert, navigate, reversible, irreversible and proposal. proposal promises that the control "commits nothing until an authority accepts". Here the AI agent proposes a match, and a user previews and selects it.

Clean: a proposal that does not act commits nothing, and the law asks no authority of it. Now the proposal acts.

Refused, under Rules 98 and 83 and Article V, and the third line of the report says so. Rule 98 lists this case among what to avoid: "Auto-applied AI corrections". The report is printed a second time as data, its machine form: this is what a person, or a tool, hands back to an AI model that writes declarations, with each rule cited by number. The repair names the authority.

Clean. Chapter 17 runs the same pair at a help desk, and one step more: the AI agent named as the authority of its own proposal, which is clean as well. The verifier reads that an authority is named. A person reads who it is.

Where a person reads

Rule 98 lists another case to avoid: "Agent-triggered irreversible operations". Here an AI agent purges the bank lines that matched nothing.

Clean: the verifier passes the case that Rule 98 lists to avoid. The role irreversible keeps no undo, by its promise, and chapter 8 tells why that is lawful. And ACTOR is a name: the verifier reads a person's name and an AI agent's alike. Here is the same purge, split as Rule 98 asks.

Both files are clean, and the difference between them is the one Article V cares about. "Never an authority above it" is held here by a person who reads the names, when the declarations are reviewed, with the rule in hand. The verifier reads the shape of the authority; a person reads who it is.

While an AI model writes

An AI model works with the law today through the verifier's command. The command checks the files named after it, zayn check orders.zayn, and with the option --json it prints the machine form above. The Zayn site describes a loop: give the law to an AI model, ask it to declare each surface before it draws it, run the verifier, and hand it the findings by rule number. In the site's words: "This loop is a procedure: the model declares, the verifier refuses by name, and the model corrects until the declaration is lawful." A refusal by rule, the page says, "lets a generator be told which law it broke instead of being told only that it was wrong". The loop ends on what the verifier reads: the exercise below shows a declaration that reaches a pass by the role it chooses, and a person reads that choice.

The roadmap names the next step: "An MCP surface serving the law to AI tools", so that AI models can consult the law while they generate. And chapter 24 shows the grammar written for a decoder, which would hold an AI model to a declaration's shape, in a form of its own.

Decisions on the record

What I refused

I deferred requiring a role on every act until evidence asks for it. On 19 August 2026 I ruled that requiring a role is, in the words of the design note on roles, "deferred to evidence"; chapter 17 tells it. It bears on this chapter: the check of Rule 98 reads the role proposal, and a file in which no control states a role passes it with a warning.

The record refuses a role that names a widget. The roles are promises about what an act does and who decides it, and the contract says the vocabulary was "Deliberately NOT sourced from Set 13, Widget Selection, whose rules prescribe widgets". The design note on roles says it in five words: "Nothing here names a widget." A proposal is a promise about who decides, never a chat bubble or a side panel.

The record refuses to merge the two authority checks. PROPOSAL_COMMITS and HIDDEN_AUTHORITY both ask for an actor, and the contract keeps both: the first "Overlaps HIDDEN_AUTHORITY in spirit and not in reach". The first is decided from the file alone, at level 2, because the role has said the act was advisory. The second needs the list of actors, at level 3. Given that list, both fire on one missing actor, each citing Rule 83, and a request of this book to the Zayn project names this double finding.

[AUTHOR: the stake of this chapter, in your words: why an AI agent is an actor under the law and never an authority above it, and what you have seen happen where it was the second.]

The court

The court of this chapter is these fixtures of the suite, each a declaration kept with the answer it must get, most of them in pairs with a twin, the same file made lawful. A proposal that acts with no authority named, and its twin that names the accountant. An act that names no actor at level 3, on a file with no medium named and on a screen; a medium is where the interface meets its user, a screen, a voice line or a program. An act with no undo, and its twin. The warning a file gets when none of its controls states a role, and its twin. And a role outside the five, and its twin. Of Set 31, the fixtures name Rule 98; a person reads the set's other rules, with each rule's number and words in hand.

Where the field leads

The field leads while the AI agent works. The Model Context Protocol sits beside the AI agent as it runs: its host "must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool", and a person "SHOULD" be able to deny a tool's call. A2UI goes further on the drawing, with parts the application registered. Zayn's service for that moment, the law served to AI tools while they work, is on its roadmap.

The field leads over time. Its guidelines speak of an AI system over many interactions: "G13: Learn from user behavior.", "G14: Update and adapt cautiously.", "G18: Notify users about changes." A declaration states one surface, and those guidelines stay with the team.

Zayn's law leads on the act. It names the AI agent as an actor. It asks each proposal that acts to name its authority, from the file alone, and each act to name its actor, at level 3, given the list of actors. The verifier refuses the declaration that breaks it before any interface is drawn, with the rule cited by number in a form the AI model that wrote it can read. Where the statute asks that a person can override or reverse a system's output, the law asks a way back on every act not declared irreversible, and a named authority on every proposal that acts; whether that authority is a person, a person reads. Where the statute asks that generated output be marked, Rule 99 asks the same of an interface, and the law files it under machine-later: a person checks the mark.

  • designedthe loop of the Zayn site in which an AI model declares, the verifier refuses by rule, and the model corrects: a procedure a person runs
  • nextthe law served to AI tools while they generate; rules for a conversation with an AI agent and for the surfaces of approval and consent

The law sets every AI agent under Article V, and Set 31 gives its rules, each with its reason and its tier word, as data. The verifier answers for Rule 98 through PROPOSAL_COMMITS, together with Rule 83, on any control that calls itself a proposal and acts; at level 3, given the actors, it answers for Rule 83 on every act. It judges a declaration by what it states, whoever wrote it and whoever acts, and this page ran it with both changed. An AI model works with the law today through the command and its machine form, in a loop that a person runs, which the Zayn site describes. The law served to AI tools while they generate, and rules for a conversation with an AI agent and for approval and consent, are next on the roadmap. The verifier reads the shape of the authority; a person reads who it is, and whether an AI agent stands where the law asks for a person, as in Rule 102.

The AI agent acts under the law. It also uses interfaces, as a person does, and the next chapter takes up that side.

Part IX · Chapter 23

The AI agent as a user

Draft

Run on 2026-11-25 01:41 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 10 of 10 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other. In an exercise those lines are kept off the page, and the answer is folded until you open it.

An AI agent as a user is a program, driven by an AI model, that operates an interface to reach a goal: it reads what the interface shows and acts through it. In this chapter I put the AI agent at the end of the interface where a person usually stands. I run one declaration on a screen and on the machine medium, the medium a program consumes, and show the same refusal. I show where Zayn's language names the one who acts, and what the law asks of an interface an AI agent operates. Then I show what the medium changes, read from the data, and what stays a person's judgment.

If you open the book here, four words come first, and every other word is said where it first appears. A declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface, a screen or any other place where a user meets the system. The law is Zayn's constitution of 123 rules for interfaces, kept as a data file. Its rules are numbered to 130, because a number taken out of use is never given again. The verifier is the program that checks a declaration against the law. A finding is one entry of the verifier's report, and a refusal when it is an error.

The field

The field's AI agents meet an interface in three ways. The first reads its pixels. Anthropic's guide to its computer use tool says the tool "provides screenshot capabilities and mouse/keyboard control for autonomous desktop interaction". OpenAI's page on its Computer-Using Agent says that screenshots are added to the AI model's context, the input it works from, and that the agent "uses a virtual mouse and keyboard to complete actions".

The second reads the interface's structure. Playwright MCP, a server that lets an AI model drive a browser, says it works "through structured accessibility snapshots, bypassing the need for screenshots". It "Uses Playwright's accessibility tree, not pixel-based input", Playwright being the program that drives the browser. The accessibility tree is W3C's term: WAI-ARIA, the web's standard for accessible controls, defines it as a "Tree of accessible objects that represents the structure of the user interface (UI)". A screen reader, the software that reads an interface aloud to a person who cannot see it, works from that structure, which the browser hands to the operating system: "Assistive technologies use the enhanced information available in an accessibility API."

The third calls the interface's own operations. The Model Context Protocol, the protocol whose letters Playwright MCP carries, connects AI models to tools and data. It gives each tool a name, a description and a schema of its input, a description of the fields the input must have. It also says: "there SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations".

And the field asks a person to confirm the act that counts. The computer use guide advises "Asking a human to confirm decisions that might result in meaningful real-world consequences". The Computer-Using Agent "seeks user confirmation for sensitive actions, such as entering login details or responding to CAPTCHA forms". Each source was read on 24 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them. So the field's AI agents operate an interface that exists, by its pixels, its structure or its tools, and the field asks a person to confirm the act.

The principle

A declaration of an interface that an AI agent operates is checked against the same rules as one a person operates; the medium it names changes what can be carried and what can be shown.

The law gives the reason in Rule 104: "What a screen reader can operate, an agent can operate and a non-visual medium can render; legibility is one law with three beneficiaries." Rule 104 holds that an interface whose structure is declared serves a person who cannot see it, an AI agent, and a medium with no screen, from the same declaration. The Zayn site draws the consequence: "An interface for an agent is an interface: the agent is the user at the other end". So this chapter puts the AI agent where the user stands, and runs it there.

One law, three beneficiaries

The law defines its user once, in its preamble, the opening text that says how the rules are read: "the operator and the user name whoever acts through an interface: the user, a person or an agent (Rule 104)". The operator is the law's own word for the user. The same sentence keeps one place for people alone: "where a rule names what is seen, heard, read or felt, it protects the person." Here is the rule it cites.

Rule 104Machine Legibility

no kind of finding of the verifier's contract
Why
What a screen reader can operate, an agent can operate and a non-visual medium can render; legibility is one law with three beneficiaries.

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

The law files Rule 104 under machine-later, its word for a rule that a program is to check, with that check to come. A medium is a way the interface meets its user. The data that describes them names 10: visual, auditory, voice, haptic, print, luminous, signage, machine, spatial and terminal. The data's row for the medium machine is titled "Consumed by a program", and its note calls it "Rule 104's third beneficiary", the medium with no screen that the rule names. On the grid of chapter 13, where the project places each rule on the activities and media it speaks of, Rule 104 is the rule placed on the machine medium. The next section runs a declaration on it.

The same refusal, two media

A declaration names its medium in SURFACE_AS, a field of a VIBE, the kind of declaration that states how a surface behaves as a whole: its medium, its density, its motion. Here is a payables desk. On a portal, a clerk schedules a supplier's payment.

Refused under Rule 79: the payment is scheduled, and the declaration keeps no way back. Now the same act through an interface for programs, where an AI agent of the payables desk schedules the payment.

The same finding, the same rule, the same right: the right to take an act back. The second report is printed twice: once as a person reads it, and once in the machine form, the report's form for a program, on any medium, with each finding's code, its line, and what it cites. This is the form a program reads before the interface exists, an AI model that writes declarations among them. The rule is cited by number, rule:79, and the right by its name, right:reverse. An AI model that wrote this declaration can read which rule it broke and repair it. The repair is the same on both media: undo within reach.

Where the user is named

The language leaves who the user is to another place. Here is a declaration that tries to state it.

A warning, and no refusal: USER is not one of the language's 10 kinds of declaration. The parenthesis of the report names the two kinds the language keeps out, WIDGET and USER. The language's specification says why: it is "a fact about who, which Zayn consumes from a symbol table rather than declares". The symbol table is a file given to the verifier beside the declaration, at level 3, that lists what the system holds. When it lists actors, the verifier asks every declaration whose SATISFIES holds ACT to name an actor; it reads that a name is there, and does not look the name up in the list. On the command line it is named after the file: zayn check payments.zayn --level 3 --symbols desk.json. A level is how much the verifier is given. The contract files each kind of finding at one of four levels: level 1 checks that the file is well formed and uses the language's own words, level 2 decides what a single declaration states, level 3 adds a table of what the system holds, and level 4 is the painted page, the page as a browser draws it. A run at a level reports the findings of the levels below it too. A declaration names the one who acts in a field, ACTOR, and a person and an AI agent are named the same way. Here is the payment again, at level 3, with the table.

Refused under Rule 83 and Article V, the law's article on authority: an act that matters names its actor. The verifier needed the table to raise it. Here is the same file at level 2, without the table.

The report prints clean: without the table, the check is silent, undecided. The repair names the AI agent.

Clean. Whether an AI agent should schedule a payment, or only propose one for the clerk to accept, is the subject of chapter 22. The verifier reads that a name is there; a person judges whether it is the right one.

What the medium changes

A medium changes two things the verifier reads: which verbs it carries, and which statuses it can show. A verb is one of the law's words for what a user does. A status is one of the words a declaration gives in SIGNALS for what a value says about its record: success, warning, danger, info and muted. Here is a statement review on a voice line, where a user hears a statement and speaks to it. Before you read the answer, say which verb a voice line cannot carry.

Two refusals. A voice line cannot zoom, and a muted status, on voice, is rendered as nothing at all. The third line of each finding lists what the contract binds to that kind of finding: its rule, an article and a right. So Rule 82 stands under Article II in one finding and Article III in the other, the articles of the two kinds; Rule 82's own article is Article III. The contract calls a verb an intent. The second fires when every status the surface declares is rendered as nothing on its medium. Now the same review through an interface for programs.

Clean, and the clean holds two different answers. The data has the machine medium carry every verb, so ZOOM passes. The statuses are another matter. The data records how a status is rendered for three media, those with a renderer built, a program that draws a declaration on that medium: visual, auditory and voice. For a medium with no entry the data says: "A medium with no entry is UNDECIDED, not 'perceptible': only channels with a shipped renderer can say." So on the machine medium the verifier decides the verbs and leaves the statuses undecided, and the report prints clean for both. The report has one word for both; a reviewer tells them apart by the medium, whose rendering the data records or leaves open.

Decisions on the record

What I refused

I refused a law of legibility with two beneficiaries. Rule 104 named two beneficiaries: a person who uses a screen reader, and an AI agent. The docket, the file where changes to the law are ruled, set the change apart for a deliberate ruling, as "the sentence the whole multi-modality argument rests on". In my pass of 13 August 2026 I adopted a third beneficiary as a correction: a medium with no screen.

I refused a law whose user is a person alone. On 7 November 2026 I answered "yes to all six" on six recommendations drawn from my remarks on the Zayn site, and one of the six made the law name whoever acts "the user, a person or an agent". It keeps one exception, in the ruling's words: "never where it names human perception". The docket gives the reason "operator" stayed: it "is the law's role word, not a description of a human".

The record keeps the user out of the language. The language states what a user does; the list of who may act belongs to the system around it.

The record refuses to call a status perceptible where no renderer can say. The machine medium's statuses stay undecided until a renderer for it is recorded.

[AUTHOR: the stake of this chapter, in your words: why an interface an AI agent operates is owed what a person is owed, and where you hold that the person stays apart.]

The court

The court of this chapter is eleven fixtures of the suite, each a declaration kept with the answer it must get, most in pairs with a twin, the same file made lawful. It holds Rule 79's undo and its twin. It holds Rule 26's cancel under SURFACE_AS machine, the suite's own pair on this medium, which chapter 12 showed. It holds the authority check at level 3, once on a file with no medium named and once on a screen, the fixture whose comment says that nothing about the medium "should change the verdict". It holds the state check at level 3. And it holds the two checks a medium changes, verbs and statuses, each with its twin. The comment of the suite's machine pair says what it leaves to a person: whether the way back "means the same thing to an API client as to a person is a judgement no verifier makes", an API client being a program that uses an interface for programs.

Run in the Zayn snapshot at commit adaecc271 on 2026-11-25 01:37 UTC+01:00. Each fixture is a declaration of the conformance suite; the suite's manifest states the findings it must get, and the run compares the two sets.

Where the field leads

The field leads on the interface that exists. Its AI agents operate a screen or a page that exists, by its pixels or its accessibility tree, and a protocol's tools with their schemas. Zayn's machine medium is a row that the data calls "derived by reasoning about each medium's properties", and the verifier reads a declaration before any surface exists.

The field leads on the person at the act. Its guides and its protocol ask a person to confirm a consequential act and to be able to deny a tool. Zayn's law holds a neighbouring line in Rule 98, which makes an AI model's output a proposal that a named authority accepts, and in the right to a human, which keeps a person reachable. The rules for the surfaces where a person approves a tool or gives consent are on its roadmap.

Zayn leads before the interface exists. An AI agent that reads pixels works from what the screen shows; one that reads the accessibility tree gets the roles a page exposes. A declaration states the verbs, the way back and the actor before the interface is drawn, and the checks this page ran refuse on the machine medium what they refuse on a screen, with the rule cited in a form a program reads.

Where it stands

  • builtthe machine medium, as a row of the media's data and in the verifier's table; the checks this page runs on it; the machine form of a report, the refusal a program reads; the actor model given at level 3, where an AI agent is named as any actor is
  • designedthe machine medium in the project's proposal for a second founding of the law; the interface through which a person meets an AI agent, in the project's architecture

Built means that it ran on this page or runs in Zayn's repository at the release named under the title. Designed means that it is specified, and that its build comes after. Next names the direction.

The machine medium is built as a row of the media's data and in the verifier's table, and it carries every verb. On it, the checks this page ran refuse what they refuse on a screen: Rule 79's undo, Rule 83's actor and the verb check there, and the suite runs Rule 26's cancel there. The machine form of the report is built, with each finding's code and citations. Who acts is named in ACTOR, a person or an AI agent alike, and given at level 3 in the table of actors. The statuses of the machine medium are undecided, and the data names the media whose rendering is recorded. The machine medium in a proposal of the project for a new base of the law, its second founding, which awaits my ruling, and the interface through which a person meets an AI agent, in the project's architecture, are designed. Next are the rules for approval and consent surfaces, and the law served to AI tools through the Model Context Protocol while they work. Whether an interface serves its AI agent well, and what a way back means to a program, is a person's judgment.

In your hands

Here is an AI agent of a shop's sales desk. Through an interface for programs it lists the orders that are late, filters them by date and scans the list, to chase each customer. The system also holds a limit on how many results the list returns. Run it at level 3 with the table, write the codes you expect, then open the verifier's answer.

Repair it, and say what you expect. Try before you read on.

Clean. The system held a limit, and the first interface did not show it: the AI agent chased the customers of a list it could not tell was cut short. Rule 82's reason, under the right to know, says what that costs: "A user who reasons from state they cannot perceive has been harmed by the interface." Now read the preamble's exception again: "where a rule names what is seen, heard, read or felt, it protects the person." Rule 82 asks that the user can perceive the state, and the verifier refused the AI agent's list all the same. Does the right to know protect an AI agent, or only the person it works for? The question is yours too, and it is among this book's requests to the Zayn project, as a question for the law.

An AI agent that operates an interface may also write one. The next chapter reads the grammar that would hold an AI model to a declaration's shape while it writes.

Part IX · Chapter 24

A grammar for generation

Draft

Run on 2026-11-25 01:41 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 11 of 11 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other. In an exercise those lines are kept off the page, and the answer is folded until you open it.

A grammar for generation is a file of rules that says which texts are declarations, so that an AI model can be held to them while it writes one. Zayn's record has one, zayn.gbnf, written by a program from the language's second declaration: the language itself declared a second time, as data, in Haro, the language of this series' first book, which chapter 9 described; it declares the language, not a surface. In this chapter I read the file beside the language's own grammar. I run one declaration in each of the two forms the record writes it in: the language's form, which the verifier reads, and the grammar's form, which a decoder would write. Then I show where the record joins the two forms, and the question that join leaves open.

If you open the book here, five words come first, and every other word is said where it first appears. A declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface. The law is Zayn's constitution of 123 rules for interfaces, kept as a data file. Its rules are numbered to 130, because a number taken out of use is never given again. The verifier is the program that checks a declaration against the law. A finding is one entry of the verifier's report, and a refusal when it is an error. An AI model is a program that writes text, here a declaration, from what it is asked.

The field

Constrained decoding is the field's name for holding an AI model to a form while it writes. A model writes its text a piece at a time, and the decoder is the part of the program that picks each next piece. A constrained decoder picks only the pieces that keep the text inside a grammar, a set of rules that says which texts are allowed, or a schema, a description of the fields a piece of data must have.

The llama.cpp project reads such grammars in a notation it calls GBNF: "a format for defining formal grammars to constrain model outputs". Its guide says that with it "you can use it to force the model to generate valid JSON", a common format for data. A rule is written name ::= ..., and "the root rule always defines the starting point of the grammar".

The providers of AI models do it with schemas. OpenAI's guide says its Structured Outputs hold a model's output "to your supplied JSON Schema", and adds that an application must still "validate any business rules that the schema does not express". Anthropic's guide says its structured outputs "guarantee schema-compliant responses through constrained decoding", and "guarantee schema compliance in most cases".

Research gives the method its measure. A paper of 2023 shows how to guide generation "with regular expressions and context-free grammars", and says it "adds little overhead": little extra work for each piece the model writes. Another, at a conference of the same year, says grammar-constrained decoding guarantees "that the output follows a given structure". A study of 2024 measured a cost: "a significant decline in LLMs reasoning abilities under format restrictions", LLMs being the large language models the field writes with.

Each source was read on 24 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them. So the field holds the shape while an AI model writes, and leaves what the text means to the program that receives it.

The principle

A grammar fixes the shape an AI model can write; what the shape means stays with the verifier.

The Zayn site says of this file: "The grammar narrows what a generator can say, and it does not make what the generator says lawful." The file's own header says it in five words: "the decoder holds the shape". The shape is a declaration's frame: a kind, a name, and the fields that kind may carry. The meaning is what the law judges: whether a verb, one of the law's words for what a user does, is the law's, and whether an act keeps its way back.

A design note of Zayn's corrected an earlier claim that said more. That claim was that the grammar makes every word that breaks the law impossible to write. The note says it "overstates what the grammar holds", and draws the line where this chapter draws it: "a misplaced field and a malformed shape are unemittable". Unemittable means that a decoder held to the grammar cannot write such a text. Every other refusal stays with the verifier.

The file and its form

The file has 29 grammar rules in GBNF. Of these, 10 each allow one kind of declaration, and each kind has a grammar rule for the fields it may carry, which the grammar calls clauses. The grammar rule root, where the grammar starts, takes one declaration or more. Every declaration the file allows has one form: DEFINE, the kind, a name, the word AS, the clauses in parentheses, then RATIONALE and a reason in quotation marks. The reason is the declaration's account of why it exists. Two of the file's grammar rules are short enough to read here:

ident ::= [a-z_] [a-z0-9_]*
ws ::= ([ \t\r\n] | "--" [^\n]* "\n")*

The first says that a name, and every word in a list, opens on a small letter or an underscore, and goes on in small letters, digits and underscores. The second says what may stand around parentheses and commas, and between declarations: spaces, tabs, line ends, and a comment that opens on two hyphens. The file's header names its form: "-- comments, double-quoted strings, UPPER_SNAKE keywords, lower_snake identifiers, trailing commas". A keyword is a word of the language, such as DEFINE, and UPPER_SNAKE means written in capitals joined by underscores; an identifier is a name the writer chooses, and lower_snake is the same in small letters; a trailing comma is a comma after the last field.

Chapter 7 gave the language's own grammar, which the verifier reads; in it a declaration is written another way. The parentheses open right after the name, with no AS. A declaration carries no RATIONALE. A comment opens on two slashes. And the law's verbs are written in capitals: the language's specification matches them "case-sensitively in their uppercase form". So the record keeps two forms of one language: the language's form, which the verifier reads, and the grammar's form, which a decoder held to this file would write.

A program writes the file from the second declaration. The same program makes the forged evaluator: a second program that judges declarations as the verifier does, made from the second declaration with no hand in between. The script of chapter 9 compares the verifier with the forged evaluator. It also writes this file again on every run, and fails when the copy kept in Zayn's repository differs.

One screen, two forms

Here is a screen of an order desk, a wholesaler's page where a clerk scans and filters the orders of the day, in the language's form. Under the plates of this section the build that makes this book prints two answers: whether the text is a sentence of the grammar, and the verifier's report.

Clean for the verifier, and not a sentence of the grammar. A sentence of a grammar is a whole text that the grammar accepts, from its first character to its last. Here the grammar meets a parenthesis where it wants AS, and the verbs are in capitals. Now the same screen in the form the grammar allows.

A sentence of the grammar, and twelve refusals from the verifier! It read DEFINE, the kind and the name, met AS where the language's grammar wants a parenthesis, and from there answered one syntax error for the parenthesis it expected, then one for each word and sign it could not place. A syntax error is the verifier's finding when a text is not written in the language's form. The contract, Zayn's file of every kind of finding the verifier may give, each bound to the law, cites no rule for it: "It is a failure to read the declaration, so no law applies". The grammar accepts one form of the screen, the verifier the other. The join comes after what each one refuses.

What the shape lets through

The grammar's lists take any name in small letters. Here is the order desk's home screen, in the grammar's form, with a verb its writer chose.

A sentence of the grammar: the grammar rule ident above takes navigate. Write the same declaration in the language's form, and the verifier reads it.

Refused: NAVIGATE is not one of the law's 22 verbs; navigate is the name of a control's role, not a verb. A decoder held to the grammar can write this verb, and the verifier refuses it once the declaration stands in the language's form. The repair uses the law's words.

Clean. A field in the wrong place is the opposite case: the grammar refuses it too. The grammar gives each kind its own grammar rule of clauses, and here is a screen's:

clause_SCREEN ::= "SATISFIES" sp namelist | "ALWAYS_REACHABLE" sp namelist | "SIGNALS" sp namelist | "ACTOR" sp ident

sp is one or more spaces and namelist a list of names in brackets; ROLE is not in it. A role is the promise a single control, an INTERACTION, makes about what acting on it does.

Refused. Now the same declaration in the grammar's form.

Not a sentence of the grammar, for the role alone: a decoder held to the grammar cannot write it. The verifier answers the form, as before.

A screen's clauses have no place for a role. Here the grammar and the verifier agree, the grammar by its shape and the verifier by its refusal. That is the design note's line: a misplaced field cannot be written, and the unknown verb stays the verifier's to refuse. The repair gives the role to the control it describes.

Clean.

Where the two forms meet

The record has a translation between the two forms, in the script of chapter 9. Its comment says what it does: a declaration "is translated MECHANICALLY" into the grammar's form. The script writes AS before the parenthesis, writes the words of every list in small letters, deletes the comments, and closes each declaration with RATIONALE "none given", because a declaration in the language's form gives no reason. The translated text goes to the forged evaluator, and the verifier reads the original. The second plate above is the first, translated, with a reason of its own in place of "none given".

So the record joins the two forms in one direction, from the language's form to the grammar's. A declaration that a decoder would write in the grammar's form must be written in the language's form before the verifier can judge it, and the exercise below takes that step by hand. Which form a decoder is to write, and which program takes a declaration from one form to the other, is a ruling the language awaits.

Decisions on the record

What I refused

A reason in the language's form. The grammar's form asks every declaration for a reason, and the second declaration says what adopting it in the language would be: "a language change, not a translation". The Zayn site records that I ruled on this difference. The second declaration dates the ruling 31 October 2026 and gives its words: "RATIONALE stays mandatory in the agent's grammar", the agent's grammar being the record's name for this file. A declaration in the language's form reaches the forged evaluator with the words "none given".

A grammar that claims more than the shape. The design note of 3 November 2026, read under the principle, is that refusal. The script says the same of the verbs: "The verbs are an identifier list and the semantic refusals stay the court's." The court, in that line, is the script's word for the forged evaluator; in this book the court is the suite.

A grammar file that drifts from its source. The script of chapter 9 refuses it, as read above: on every run it writes the file again and fails on a difference.

[AUTHOR: the stake of this chapter, in your words: why an AI model should be held to the shape of a declaration while it writes, and what you want the reason it gives to become.]

The court

The court of this chapter is five fixtures of the suite, each a declaration kept with the answer it must get. Two are the refusals the plates met: an unknown verb and a role on a screen. Two are a flow that acts and its lawful twin, which the exercise meets. The contract files each kind of finding at one of four levels: level 1 checks that the file is well formed and uses the language's own words, level 2 decides what a single declaration states, level 3 adds a table of what the system holds, and level 4 is the painted page, the page as a browser draws it. A run at a level reports the findings of the levels below it too. The unknown verb is a word outside the law's, so level 1 refuses it; every report on this page is at level 2. The last shows the language's form at its loosest, with comments on two slashes, a comma after the last field and an empty body, and the verifier accepts it.

The suite pins the language and leaves syntax errors to each verifier, with its reason: "Recovery is not part of the language." Recovery is what a verifier reports after the first word or sign it cannot place. So the counts of syntax errors on this page are this verifier's.

Run in the Zayn snapshot at commit adaecc271 on 2026-11-25 01:37 UTC+01:00. Each fixture is a declaration of the conformance suite; the suite's manifest states the findings it must get, and the run compares the two sets.

  • unknown-intent.zaynUNKNOWN_INTENTanswers as the manifest expects
  • role-misplaced.zaynROLE_MISPLACEDanswers as the manifest expects
  • comments-and-formatting.zaynno findinganswers as the manifest expects
  • missing-cancel.zaynMISSING_CANCELanswers as the manifest expects
  • missing-cancel-lawful.zaynno findinganswers as the manifest expects

The codes above, in the words of the verifier's contract

  • UNKNOWN_INTENTlevel 1, errorA verb in SATISFIES or ALWAYS_REACHABLE is not one of the 22.
  • ROLE_MISPLACEDlevel 2, errorROLE is declared on a kind that is not an INTERACTION.
  • MISSING_CANCELlevel 2, errorA flow that acts cannot be abandoned: ALWAYS_REACHABLE lacks CANCEL.

Where the field leads

The field leads in the decoder. Its grammars and schemas are read by decoders that run, in the programs that run AI models and in the providers' services. The field's decoders read GBNF, the notation of this file; a decoder that holds an AI model to it within Zayn's own loop is next.

Zayn leads in the second layer, the meaning. OpenAI's guide leaves what a schema does not express to the application, which must "validate any business rules". For an interface, Zayn names those rules: a law, a verifier that refuses by the rule or the article it cites, and a court of fixtures against which the verifier's refusals are proved. An AI model can read the verifier's report on the language's form, and chapter 22 describes the Zayn site's loop, a procedure a person runs, in which one does.

And the field measures the price of a held form. The study of 2024 found that reasoning declined under format restrictions, and, in reasoning tasks, generally more as the format tightens. That is the loss beside the win: a form held while an AI model writes can cost some of what it writes, and the field measures it.

Where it stands

  • builta grammar for constrained decoding, as a file of 29 grammar rules written by a program from the language's second declaration, and compared on every run of the record's script with a fresh copy; a translation from the language's form into the grammar's; the verifier, which reads the language's form
  • designedthe generate workflow of the Zayn site: a grammar for the shape and the verifier for the meaning, in a loop that a person runs with an AI model; the second declaration's places for the menu fields of language 1.6
  • nexta decoder that holds an AI model to the grammar; the law served to an AI model while it writes; the ruling on which written form that decoder writes

Built means that it ran on this page or runs in Zayn's repository at the release named under the title. Designed means that it is specified, and that its build comes after. Next names the direction.

Built: the grammar for generation, as a file of 29 grammar rules. A program writes it from the language's second declaration, and the script of chapter 9 writes it again and compares it on every run, where the Haro forge, the program that makes an evaluator and this file from the second declaration, is installed. The same script has the translation from the language's form to the grammar's. The verifier reads the language's form, and this page ran every plate on it.

Designed: the generate workflow of the Zayn site, the grammar for the shape and the verifier for the meaning, in a loop that a person runs with an AI model. The language has versions of its own, and its specification in this release is at version 1.7. The second declaration names version 1.4 of the language, and the grammar written from it carries the 10 kinds and their clauses as of that version; the menus of version 1.6 are written in the language's form, and their places in the second declaration are designed.

Next: a decoder that holds an AI model to the grammar, the law served to an AI model while it writes, and the ruling on which form that decoder writes.

In your hands

This exercise is written for the book: a declaration in the grammar's form, as a decoder held to the grammar would write it for the order desk. It releases an order for shipping. Say what you expect from the verifier, and why, then open its answer.

A sentence of the grammar. The verifier read the name, answered the syntax errors, then a warning that the flow lists no verbs: it judged the declaration as a name with no fields. Every line of the report is about the form. Write the declaration in the language's form, keep the reason in a comment, and run it again. Try before you read on.

Now the law speaks. Repair it, and say what you expect. Try before you read on.

Clean. The first form is the grammar's, and the verifier's report on it is about the form; the verifier judged the law on the second and the third. Which form would you have a decoder write, and where would its reason live once the declaration stands in the language's form?

The verifier is a command, and a team can run it at the gate where its work is checked before it ships. Part X starts there.

Part X · Chapter 25

The command and the gate

Draft

Run on 2026-11-25 01:41 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 11 of 11 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other. In an exercise those lines are kept off the page, and the answer is folded until you open it.

The command is the verifier as a program a team runs by typing its name, and the gate is the step of a team's build where it runs, so that a declaration that breaks the law stops the build. A build is the chain of commands that turns a team's files into a product. It stops when one command ends with any number but 0, and that number is the command's exit code. In this chapter I read the command as the record, Zayn's repository at its release, holds it. I run the reference command on the three values of that number, and I describe the release, the command's published files, as its notes record it. Then I show what a team chooses: the level of the check, the table of what the system holds, and the files.

If you open the book here, four words come first, and every other word is said where it first appears. A declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface. The law is Zayn's constitution of 123 rules for interfaces, kept as a data file; its rules are numbered to 130, because a number taken out of use is never given again. The verifier is the program that checks a declaration against the law. A finding is one entry of the verifier's report, and a refusal when it is an error.

A declaration names its kind and its name, then lists its clauses. The kinds on this page are a SCREEN, an addressable surface; a FORM, a conversation with the system; an INTENT_FLOW, the steps of one intent, such as submitting a week; and an INTERACTION, an act bound to an object, such as a control. SATISFIES lists the law's verbs that the user performs there, such as READ, SELECT, CONFIRM and ACT. ALWAYS_REACHABLE lists the verbs kept within reach at every step, such as UNDO and CANCEL. ROLE states the promise a control makes about acting on it, in one of five words: inert, it informs; navigate, it changes what is shown; reversible, it changes what is true and can be taken back; irreversible, it changes what is true for good; proposal, it commits nothing until an authority accepts it. A plate is a declaration shown with its run, and its lines that begin //--> are comments the verifier skips.

The field

The field's gates read one number. Git, the program that records a team's changes, runs a hook, a script of the team's, before each change is recorded. Its documentation says of the pre-commit hook: "Exiting with a non-zero status from this script causes the git commit command to abort before creating a commit." The same hook "can be bypassed with the --no-verify option". The pre-commit project, "A framework for managing and maintaining multi-language pre-commit hooks", gives the reason teams use them: "Git hook scripts are useful for identifying simple issues before submission to code review." So the first gate stands before a change is recorded.

A shared copy of a project can stop a change in the same way. Continuous integration, CI, is a service that runs a team's build on every change sent to that shared copy. GitHub's documentation says of a protected branch with required checks: "all required status checks must pass before collaborators can merge changes into the protected branch". And of an action, one step of such a build, an exit code of 0 means "The action completed successfully and other tasks that depend on it can begin"; "Any other exit code indicates the action failed." The second gate stands before a change joins the others.

The tools decide what their number means. ESLint, a program that checks code, gives "error" an exit code of 1 and lets "warn" leave it untouched, and a team can go further with --max-warnings, which "can be used to force ESLint to exit with an error status if there are too many warning-level rule violations". And the field shares one format for findings. SARIF, a standard of the OASIS consortium, "defines a standard format for the output of static analysis tools", and "GitHub can parse SARIF files produced by third-party tools to display code scanning alerts in repositories."

Each source was read on 21 and 24 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them. So the field's gate stops on a number, and the tool behind it decides which findings move the number.

The principle

A gate reads one number: 1 when the verifier refused a declaration, 0 when it refused none, even with warnings, and 2 when it could not open what it was given; the build goes on at 0 alone.

The reference command's own guide says it in two lines: "Exit codes: 0 clean · 1 violations found · 2 usage or read error. That is all a CI gate needs." A gate set to read a table of what the system holds needs one thing more, that table, as the section on a team's choices shows. Zayn belongs to a family of languages built the same way, each with its own law and its own verifier, which the family calls a court. The family's Diagnostic Contract sets the shape every one of them gives a finding, and gives each severity, error or warning, its meaning. An error means "the artifact is unlawful; a build must fail"; a warning means "lawful but suspect, or undecidable without more input". The report is for a person; the machine form, the same findings printed for a program, is for a tool; and the number is for the build.

The command, as released

The command has two programs in the record. The reference is a program in JavaScript, run with Node, the program that runs JavaScript outside a browser, as node tools/zayn/cli.js check in a copy of the repository. This book runs it on every plate, and it answers one verb, check. The zayn command is the same verifier written again as one file for each operating system, written to print byte for byte what the reference prints, which a script of the record compares. The command lines of this page run the reference under the command's name, and a file it cannot read is told in the reference's own words.

A verb of the command is the first word after its name, and an option, a word that begins with two hyphens such as --level 3, changes how the verb works. The first lines of the command's source list its verbs. check is the verifier. conformance runs the suite: the declarations the record keeps, each with the answer it must get, which are called its fixtures. pack writes or checks the manifest of the files a team pins, that is, records by their hash, so that it uses one edition. cross-medium compares one declaration's renderings in two media. audit-facts reads the facts of the audit of screenshots, serve serves the site and its audit, site runs the site's own checks, and version names the editions of the law, the language and the contract that the command carries; the option --version names the release.

The release 0.2.0 carries the law at version 3.17, the language at 1.7, and the contract at 1.11. The contract is the file that binds each kind of finding to the law and places it at a level; the family's Diagnostic Contract is another file, the shape of a finding. The release notes list its files.

A file's name says the system it runs on: x86_64 and aarch64 name the two families of processor, and SHA-256 is the kind of hash, a long number computed from a file's bytes. The .wasm file is the verifier built for a browser, the one the Zayn site runs on its pages. The notes say how to know a file: "The hash is how to know a file is the one built here." The same bytes give the same number. And they say what to do when the check of a file's hash fails: "A file that prints FAILED is not the one built here: do not run it." This book runs the reference command in its build, and tells the release's files as their notes record them.

One number, three values

The gate's one number has three values, the command's answers to a build: 1, 0 and 2. Here each is run on a timesheet desk, where an employee enters the hours of the week and submits them, and a manager reviews the team's weeks. A change to its declarations reaches the gate.

Refused, under Rule 16: a screen the user reads also acts. The contract states the invariant: "A read surface that silently acts is an intent violation." The command answers 1, and the build stops. A tool reads the same refusal in the machine form, with the option --json:

At the command line
$ zayn check week.zayn --json
{
  "level": 2,
  "contract": {
    "version": "1.11",
    "constitution": "3.17"
  },
  "files": [
    "week.zayn"
  ],
  "counts": {
    "errors": 1,
    "warnings": 0

  "diagnostics": [
    {
      "code": "READ_ACT_COLLAPSE",
      "severity": "error",
      "message": "A reading surface mutates: SATISFIES holds READ and ACT.",
      "span": {
        "file": "week.zayn",
        "line": 1
      },
      "cites": [
        "rule:16",
        "article:intent"

      "language": "zayn",

      "subject": "timesheet_week"

Each finding is one object under diagnostics: its code, its severity, its message, its span, the file and the line where it stands, and what it cites, the rule by its number and the article by its name, which the person's report prints as a numeral. Then its language, its level, the level the contract gives its kind, and the subject, the name it judges. The repair puts the act on a flow of its own: the week is read on one screen, and submitting it opens steps of its own, where the user selects, confirms, and can go back.

Clean, and the command answers 0. In the machine form the answer is the same object with no finding in it. With --quiet the command prints a person's report, findings only, and a clean run prints nothing. Here are both:

In the machine form a clean run still prints its list of findings, under diagnostics, empty. The family's Diagnostic Contract requires it: "Clean and no output are different facts". Now a finding that is a warning.

A warning, and the command answers 0. The build goes on, and its log, the text the build prints as it runs, keeps the warning for a person to read. The flow is declared in the file of the second plate. Here are the two files checked in one run:

At the command line
$ zayn check week.zayn entry.zayn
entry.zayn:1  warning  UNRESOLVED_INTENT_FLOW  submit_week referenced by week_entry
    An INTENT_FLOW reference names no declared flow.

0 error(s), 1 warning(s) across 2 file(s) at level 2

exit code 0run: the command returned the exit code this page states

The warning stays: the verifier judges each file on its own, and the next section shows what that means for a project. Now a file the verifier reads and cannot parse.

A syntax error, at the line where the file ends, and the command answers 1. A file the verifier reads and cannot parse, that is, cannot read in the language's grammar, is a refusal. Here is a file name with no file behind it:

At the command line
$ zayn check sheet.zayn
zayn: cannot read sheet.zayn: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'sheet.zayn'

exit code 2run: the command returned the exit code this page states

2: the command could not open what it was given, a read error in its own words. So the gate's one number has three values, and each is a different message: 1, a declaration broke the law or the language's grammar; 0, none did; 2, the gate itself was set wrong.

What a team chooses

A team chooses the level, the table and the files the gate checks. A level is how much the verifier is given. The contract places each kind of finding at one of four levels. Level 1 checks that the file is well formed and uses the language's own words. Level 2 decides what the file alone states, its declarations read together. Level 3 adds a table of what the system holds. Level 4 is the painted page, the page as a browser draws it. The contract places one kind of finding there, content that "reserves no space and shoves the reading when it lands". Its note gives that kind to the audit of the painted page, a program that measures the page in a browser, which chapter 26 shows. A run at a level reports the findings of the levels below it too, so a run at level 4 runs every check the verifier holds. The command runs at level 2 unless it is told another.

The symbol table, the table for short, is a small file, given with --symbols, that lists what the system around a declaration holds under four keys, named entities, actors, state and elements. The two checks of this chapter read two of them: actors for an act's actor, and state for what a surface must show. A team writes the table by hand today; a table computed from the project is the work the record names next. Here is the second plate's file, word for word, at level 3 with the project's table.

Two refusals where level 2 found none: the act names no actor, and the status of the week is shown nowhere. The verifier's messages say operator, the language's word for the person this book calls the user. The level a team sets changes what its gate stops. Here is the same file at level 3, with no table:

At the command line
$ zayn check week.zayn --level 3
clean — 1 file(s), 0 violations at level 3 against Zayn v3.17

exit code 0run: the command returned the exit code this page states

Clean, and the command answers 0. Without the table, the checks of level 3 have nothing to read, and they say nothing. The command's own help says it: "undecidable is silence, never a pass". The silence is the verifier's, and the 0 is the gate's: the report and the machine form of this run are those of a clean file, and a gate reads them as a pass. So a gate set at level 3 is given its table on the same command line. Here is the repair, checked with the project's table, as the plate before was.

Clean. Now the files. A project keeps its declarations in several files, and the record's build step checks them in one run: zayn check specs/*.zayn, where the star stands for any name, every .zayn file in the folder specs. Here are two files of the project, the screens and the flows, each checked at level 3 with the project's table.

The flows file is refused for a state that the screens file shows. Here are the two checked together, in one run:

At the command line
$ zayn check screens.zayn flows.zayn --level 3 --symbols project.json
flows.zayn  error  INVISIBLE_STATE  week_status
    The system holds state the operator must know, and no surface declares showing it.
    Rule 82 · Perceivable State · Article III · the right to know

1 error(s), 0 warning(s) across 2 file(s) at level 3

exit code 1run: the command returned the exit code this page states

Each file keeps the answer it gets alone: the screens clean, the flows refused. At level 3 the verifier reads each file with the whole system's table: the table speaks for the project, and the file for itself. So a team that gates at level 3 keeps a flow and the screen that shows its state in one file, as the repaired week does, and the gate passes. Which the gate should read, one file or the project's declarations together, is a question this book puts to the Zayn project.

Decisions on the record

What I refused

I refused the law a web address until someone outside asks to cite it; until then its hash names it. On 18 August 2026 I ruled, in the words the pack's guide records: "The pack stays content-addressed. Buy a domain when the first outside citation is asked for." Content-addressed means named by its hash. The pack is the set of files a team pins. The law is one file and the language four. The contract is one, and the family's Diagnostic Contract two, with the file of its shape. Two files hold the media an interface can be rendered in and what each medium carries, and two hold the proof: the suite's manifest and the cases of the comparison across media. That is 12 files, with a manifest of the pack, MANIFEST.json, the list that gives each file's hash. The guide tells a team what to do with it: "Vendor the twelve files, record MANIFEST.json beside them, and make zayn pack --check a step in your build." To vendor is to copy the files into the team's own project. "A version number says which edition you meant. A hash says the bytes you have are that edition."

The record refuses a manifest that rewrites itself when the files change. "The manifest never regenerates itself": the pack's tool writes it only when asked, "because a manifest that follows the tree automatically pins nothing". The tree is the folder of files the manifest lists.

The record refuses a third severity. The family's Diagnostic Contract ranks its two severities as rungs, and a court in its words is one verifier of the family: "A third rung is a substance change to this contract, never a court's private extension." A gate has two answers about the law, a refusal or a pass.
