Set 13 · Widget Selection

Opinionated selection of business-focused widgets with clear use cases

Rule 45Text Editing: Auto-expanding Plaintext

For business notes and descriptions: Auto-expanding plaintext or Markdown fields. Editing happens in-place. No "Save" button for text; we use "Blur-to-Save." Assumes trust in the user's intent. Markdown separates structure of thought from decoration.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
judgment
Avoid
WYSIWYG editors with 20+ icons; Modal dialogs for text editing; Separate "Save" buttons for text fields
Why
In-place plaintext with blur-to-save keeps writing where thinking is.
Rule 46Date Selection: Semantic Text Input

A text field that accepts ISO (YYYY-MM-DD) or semantic shortcuts ("today", "+7d"). A small calendar icon exists only as a fallback. Tip text: "Type '+30' for thirty days from now." Sequence over grid: Typing is faster than clicking for power users.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
machine-later
Avoid
Calendar pickers requiring 4+ clicks; Forcing date format compliance without guidance; No support for natural language dates
Why
Typing 'today' beats four clicks in a grid; dates are language before they are calendars.
Rule 47Numbers: Monospaced Input

Use monospaced fonts with tabular-nums (tnum) feature for all numbers and currency. Always right-align numeric columns. Include unit suffixes ("USD", "%") for immediate context. The Alignment Law: Numbers must use tabular-nums for vertical comparison.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
machine-later
Avoid
Variable-width fonts for currency; Left-aligned numeric columns; No unit suffixes for context
Why
Tabular digits are how columns admit comparison.
Rule 48Tables: High-Density Ledger

The Ledger: High-density row-striped grid for transaction logs and client lists. Low-contrast borders prevent the "jail-cell" effect. Action buttons remain hidden until row hover. The 8-Hour Test: Designed for extended viewing without eye strain.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Card-based layouts for tabular data; Excessive padding that wastes space; Zebra striping on small tables
Why
Operators read tables for eight hours; density with low noise is mercy, not clutter.
Rule 49Calendar: Vertical Agenda View

Vertical Agenda View for scheduling and audit trails. Linearity: Business is a sequence of events. Monthly grids are for "planning"; Agendas are for "doing." Show only relevant events with clear time indicators.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Monthly grid views for task management; Cluttered date cells with too much information; No focus on current tasks
Why
Business time is a sequence; grids are for planning, agendas for doing.
Rule 50Charts: Tufte-style Sparklines

Tufte-style Sparklines for trend analysis and KPIs. Data-to-Ink Ratio: No 3D, no legends, no axes unless strictly required for truth. Monochrome with single accent color for emphasis. No pie charts—bar charts enable direct comparison. If a user needs exact numbers, they hover.

Article
I · Calm
Tier
judgment
Avoid
3D pie charts; Excessive legends and axes; Bright colors that compete for attention
Why
Ink that is not data is noise; comparison beats decoration.
Rule 119A Card Is Not a Button

Form follows role, and each widget plays exactly one. A card is a read-only indicator -- KPI, summary, state -- with no call to action inside it. An action takes the shape of a button or a link: distinct background, honest affordance. And repetitive data with coherent attributes is a table, never a card grid -- five records with the same five fields are rows, whatever the fashion says. A surface that blurs these roles makes the operator test every element to learn what it does.

Article
II · Intent Over Mechanics
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Clickable tiles styled like information cards; A KPI card with a chevron pretending to be read-only; Repetitive rows with identical attributes laid out as a grid of cards; A decorative pipeline strip that looks pressable
Why
When everything might be pressable, the operator must poke the interface to learn it -- and an interface learned by poking is an interface that was never read.

Set 14 · Focus Mode

Visual isolation for deep concentration on critical tasks

Rule 51The Cognitive Tunnel

Focus Mode is visual isolation. When engaged, a high-opacity scrim covers the rest of the interface. Only the active container remains at 100% opacity. Everything else is blurred and desaturated. Pointer events for the background are disabled. Esc key always exits.

Article
II · Intent Over Mechanics
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Modal dialogs that don't dim the background; Side panels that remain visible during focus tasks; Notifications that appear during intensive work
Why
Focus is spatial; the world must visibly wait, not vanish.
Rule 52The Scrim

The scrim should have 40% opacity with backdrop-filter: blur(8px). This creates sufficient visual separation without causing nausea. The active container should have a subtle border (2px solid primary color) and box-shadow to enhance the spotlight effect.

Article
I · Calm
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Transparent overlays that don't obscure background; Blur effects that cause motion sickness; Inconsistent scrim opacity across the application
Why
A consistent scrim isolates without nausea and without pretending the world is gone.
Rule 53Interaction Lockdown

Pointer events for the background are disabled during Focus Mode. Only the focused container and its children are interactive. The Esc key is the universal exit path. A subtle "Exit Focus (Esc)" hint should be visible in the container header.

Article
II · Intent Over Mechanics
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Clickable background elements during focus mode; Keyboard shortcuts that exit focus unexpectedly; No clear exit path from focus mode
Why
A focus that can be escaped only by luck is a trap; Esc is the covenant.

Set 15 · Circadian Theming

Ocular preservation through thoughtful day/night mode implementation

Rule 54Night Mode Ocular Preservation

Night Mode is ocular preservation, not color inversion. Use deep charcoals (#1a1a1a) instead of pure black. Use soft grays (#e0e0e0) instead of pure white. Reduce contrast ratios slightly. Desaturate warning/error colors so they don't "glow" painfully. Respect prefers-color-scheme but allow manual override.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Pure black (#000000) backgrounds; Pure white (#FFFFFF) text on dark backgrounds; High-contrast "glowing" colors in night mode
Why
Night work is real work; inverted glare is not preservation.
Rule 55Low-Blue Law

In Night Mode, shift color temperature toward warmer tones. Reduce blue light emission in accent colors. Primary color should be softer (e.g., #60a5fa instead of #3b82f6). This reduces eye strain during extended night sessions.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Bright blue accents in night mode; Cool color temperatures that disrupt circadian rhythm; No reduction in blue light emission
Why
Blue at midnight taxes the body that must return at eight.
Rule 56Semantic Preservation

Warning (Gold) and Error (Oxblood) must remain recognizable but should be desaturated so they don't "glow" painfully. Ensure all text maintains minimum 4.5:1 contrast ratio even in night mode. Semantic meaning must be preserved across themes -- and across the reading of whoever receives it: what a declaration fixes is the meaning, and the rendering is derived per theme, per medium and per culture. The cultural clause binds once a meaning-to-rendering path exists to obey it.

Article
III · Visible State
Tier
machine-later
Avoid
Colors that lose meaning in night mode; Inconsistent semantic mapping between themes; Accessibility contrast violations in night mode

Set 16 · Visual Business Flows

Representing business logic visually without cluttering the mind

Rule 57The Wayline

Business flows should be visible at the top of the "River," showing where the current document sits in the grander lifecycle. Non-Blocking Logic: The flow should be visible but not obstructive. Interactive Nodes: Clicking a previous node should scroll the user back to that historical data—treating the flow as a Time-Travel Navigation tool.

Article
III · Visible State
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Linear progress bars that hide complexity; Static flow diagrams that don't reflect current state; No interaction with flow visualization
Why
A document that shows its place in the lifecycle answers the meeting's first question.
Rule 58Living Diagram Principle

Flows are "Living Diagrams" that reflect real-time state. Completed steps show solid lines with checkmarks. Active steps have subtle pulsing or bold borders. Future steps use dashed lines and semi-transparent text. The diagram updates automatically as the workflow progresses.

Article
III · Visible State
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Static images of business processes; Diagrams that don't update with state changes; No connection between diagram and actual data
Why
A diagram that lies about state is worse than none.
Rule 59State Visualization

Completed: Solid line, quiet checkmark. Active: Pulsing (subtle) or bold border—the only "moving" part of a Calm UI. Future: Dashed line, semi-transparent text. Impact Statement: Button shows downstream consequence ("Approving unlocks $2M procurement budget").

Article
III · Visible State
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Unclear indication of current workflow step; No visual distinction between completed and pending steps; Missing impact statements for each step
Why

Set 17 · Accessibility

Accessibility as an extension of cognitive mercy

Rule 60Screen Reader Harmony

The interface exposes its structure to assistive technology: semantic landmarks that can be navigated, a descriptive label for every icon and complex widget, and non-interrupting announcement of updates such as stzErrors. On the web this is realized with <main>, <nav>, <section>, aria-label, aria-describedby and aria-live="polite" -- that is the realization, not the rule. A voice assistant, a phone tree, an embedded panel or any screen reader outside the web owes the same structure by its own means.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
machine
Avoid
Non-semantic HTML structure; Missing ARIA labels for interactive elements; aria-live regions that interrupt user flow
Why
The interface must speak to those who cannot see it; semantics is how, in whatever medium it speaks.
Rule 62Contrast & Legibility

Maintain minimum 4.5:1 contrast ratio for text, even in night mode. Use rem and em units to respect user's browser font settings. Test with grayscale mode to ensure information hierarchy remains clear without color.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
tool
Avoid
Insufficient color contrast ratios; Fixed font sizes (px instead of rem/em); Text that doesn't scale with browser settings
Why
Text that ignores user settings excludes the users who set them.
Rule 105The Legibility Floor

Main reading text is at least 1rem with generous line height, and never lighter than 4.5:1 against its background; long-form prose aims for 7:1. Secondary text may be quieter in size or weight -- never in legibility. If a color carries meaning, it must also carry contrast.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
tool
Avoid
Body text below 1rem; Muted grays that fail 4.5:1 contrast against their background; Accent-colored text that fails contrast on light backgrounds; Meaning conveyed by faintness
Why
Text you must lean into is text you will misread -- faintness is not a design language, it is a tax on every reader.

Set 18 · Multilingualism & Dialects

Supporting linguistic and business context diversity

Rule 63Business Dialect Switching

A "User" may be a "Client" in a CRM module but a "Debtor" in a Finance module. Dynamic Aliasing: The UI should support a dictionary where labels change based on the active Business Context. Omnibar Integration: Use Ctrl+K > "Dialect: Logistics" to instantly rename headers across the app (e.g., "Amount" becomes "Freight Cost").

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Fixed terminology that doesn't adapt to context; No support for domain-specific language; Forcing users to learn system terminology
Why
Operators think in their domain's words; the UI should learn them, not teach its own.
Rule 64Right-to-Left Logic

True multilinguism requires Bi-Directional Calm. Mirroring the River: For RTL languages (Arabic, Hebrew), the 70/30 axis mirrors. The "Ma" (negative space) flows from the left. Logical Spacing: Use CSS Logical Properties (e.g., margin-inline-start instead of margin-left) so the "Calm" spacing persists regardless of direction. What must NOT mirror: clocks, media transport controls, the digits within a number, and any progress that encodes a physical direction. Mirroring the layout axis is not mirroring the world.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Hard-coded left/right margins; Icons that don't flip in RTL mode; Text alignment that doesn't adapt
Why
Calm that only flows left-to-right is not calm; it is locale bias.
Rule 122Language Is Data

Every human-readable string lives in a per-language dictionary file; the code references keys, and the dictionary is the single source of truth. Adding a language -- Wolof, Hausa, Bambara, Zarma, Arabic -- means adding a file and registering a locale, never touching code. And a localized interface speaks its language whole: when the UI is French, 'workflow' is 'parcours', 'monitoring' is 'supervision', 'legacy' is 'patrimoine' -- jargon imported untranslated reserves the interface for developers and shuts out the operators it was written for.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Strings hard-coded in markup or logic; A second language added by forking templates; Localized UI that keeps the source language's technical jargon; Strings duplicated between code and dictionary
Why
The constitution is data so the law cannot drift from the linter; language is data for the same reason -- and because the next operator's mother tongue should cost a file, not a fork.

Set 19 · Boardroom Mode

Presentation-ready views for management meetings and stakeholder reviews

Rule 65Structural Slicing

The h2 Breakpoint: Every h2 or section tag is treated as the start of a new "Slide." UI Stripping: All navigation, sidebars, and "Noise" (buttons/inputs) are hidden. Only the Artifacts (Charts, Tables, Text) remain. Scaling for Distance: Fonts automatically scale by 150% to ensure legibility from the back of a meeting room.

Projecting full application UI in meetings; Cluttered screens with navigation chrome; Tiny text unreadable from distance

The Laser Pointer: A custom cursor (large, high-contrast) for the presenter. Live-Data Refresh: Unlike static PowerPoint, the "Slides" are live widgets. You can update a value in a table, and the chart reflects it instantly during the meeting. Navigation: Arrow keys move between slides; Esc exits presentation mode.

Set 20 · Mobile Adaptation

Thumb-driven interface design for mobile business applications

Rule 67The Law of the Thumb

On mobile, the top 30% of the screen is a "dead zone" for the thumb. The Bottom Command Bar: The Omnibar and primary actions move to the bottom of the viewport. The Header as a Label: The top of the screen is strictly for Orientation (the Breadcrumb). It is for the eyes, not the fingers.

Top navigation bars on mobile; Tiny targets requiring precision tapping; Ignoring thumb reach zones

Rule 68Bottom Sheet Focus

Instead of centering a "Modal" in the middle of the screen (forcing a reach), we use Bottom Sheets. Gesture-Native: These are invoked from the bottom and dismissed by swiping down—mimicking the natural physics of a scroll. Include a drag handle at the top for affordance.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Centered modals requiring reach; No gesture support for mobile interactions; Desktop patterns forced onto mobile screens

Rule 69The Hand Is Not a Mouse

No Tiny Targets: Every interactive element has a minimum height of 48px to prevent "fat-finger" errors. The "Bounce" Limit: While we allow natural scrolling, we disable "Overscroll-Bounce" on internal containers to prevent the UI from feeling like it's "shaking." Swipe Actions: For the Ledger (Table), implement Swipe-to-Action (e.g., swipe right to archive).

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes

Avoid
Overscroll bounce on internal containers; No visual feedback on touch interactions; Inconsistent tap targets across the application

Set 21 · Settings

Configuration interfaces that minimize cognitive overhead

Rule 70The Monastery of Configuration

Treat settings as a Searchable Library. The Flat Hierarchy: Avoid 4-level deep menus. Use broad categories (General, Security, Billing) and let the Omnibar handle the rest. The "Contextual Save": For critical business settings, use a "Pending Changes" bar at the bottom. This prevents the micro-anxiety of wondering if a toggle was saved instantly or if it needs a "Confirm" click.

Every setting must have a one-sentence "Why." Bad: Enable Log Rotation [Toggle]. Calm: Log Rotation: Automatically clears history every 30 days to keep the system fast. [Toggle]. Explain the business impact, not just the technical function.

When viewing a document or diagram, the UI chrome (sidebar, top-nav) should recede by 50% opacity or slide away entirely. Set 23 · User Management

Interfaces for managing people and permissions with dignity

Rule 74The Face & Role Trinity

People are not "Records"; they are actors in the system. The "Face & Role" Trinity: A user list should always show: Who (Avatar/Name), What (Role/Permissions), and Status (Active/Away/Inactive). Use status dots (green for active, gray for away) for quick scanning.

Rule 75Permission Sliders

For complex business roles, use "Access Levels" (None → Read → Write → Admin) rather than a confusing grid of checkboxes. Visual sliders or segmented controls make permission assignment intuitive and reduce cognitive load.

When changing roles for 50 users, show one quiet progress bar. Do not send 50 individual "Success" notifications. Batch operations should be efficient and unobtrusive, respecting the user's focus.

Set 24 · Business Document Anatomy

Standardized structure for business documents like bills and purchase orders

Rule 77The Trinity Structure

Whether it's a Bill, a Quote, or a PO, every document follows the Document Trinity: The Header (Identity): Logo, Date, Document Number (Top-Left/Right). The Body (The Meat): The Table/Ledger of items. (Rule 11, The Ledger Principle, applies here). The Footer (Conclusion): Totals, Terms, and the "Call to Action" (Signature/Approve). This ensures consistency and professionalism across all business documents.

Set 25 · The Zayn Litmus Test

Final validation checklist before shipping any screen or feature

Rule 78The Grand Unified Test

Before shipping an interface, it must pass: Context: Does terminology match the user's role (Dialect)? Continuity: Does the page flow logically from top-to-bottom (The River)? Resilience: Does it handle errors without jumping (stzErrors)? Inclusivity: Is it accessible and RTL-ready? Scale: Can it be projected in a boardroom with one button press? Additionally, ask these questions: • Can I understand this without instructions? • Is anything trying to attract attention unnecessarily? • Is the most important thing obvious in 3 seconds? • Would removing something make it calmer? • Would I enjoy maintaining this UI in 2 years? • Can a user look at this for 8 hours without a headache? • If printed in black and white, would it still be functional? • Can a new employee perform basic tasks without a manual?

Article
VII · Amendment
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Shipping interfaces without user validation; Ignoring accessibility requirements; Focusing on aesthetics over usability
Why
A law that cannot be tested at the door will be negotiated in the hallway.

Set 26 · Action Reversibility

Trust-based undo system that respects user flow

Rule 79The Undo Covenant

Every destructive action (delete, archive, clear) must have instant, one-click undo for 10 seconds via a toast notification. No confirmation dialogs for common operations—just immediate reversal. Show 'Deleted 3 items. [Undo]' at bottom of screen. Trust users, respect their flow. Confirmation dialogs reserved only for irreversible system-level operations (purge database, revoke credentials).

Article
IV · Reversibility
Tier
machine
Avoid
Confirmation dialogs for every deletion; No way to reverse common destructive actions; Undo buried in menus or requiring multiple steps; Breaking workflow with confirmation dialogs
Why
Undo trusts first and interrupts never; confirmation interrupts always and trusts nothing.

Set 27 · Keyboard Primacy

Power users should never be forced to reach for the mouse

Rule 80Keyboard Sovereignty

Every primary action must have a visible keyboard shortcut displayed next to it. Tab order must follow visual hierarchy (left-to-right, top-to-bottom). Arrow keys navigate tables/lists. Enter confirms, Escape cancels universally. Function keys (F1-F12) for mode switching. Shortcuts should be mnemonic where possible (Ctrl+S = Save, not Ctrl+Q). A global '?' key reveals all shortcuts in context. Focus is always visible (a clear ring, never outline: none), tab order follows the visual river, and a "Skip to Content" link appears on focus.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
machine
Avoid
Hidden keyboard shortcuts; Illogical tab order; Critical actions only accessible via mouse; Tooltip-only shortcut documentation; outline: none on focusable elements; Missing skip links for keyboard users
Why
The keyboard is the operator's instrument; any critical act that requires the mouse demotes the expert.

Set 28 · Time & Async Clarity

Time as the operator lives it: loading states that inform, and interfaces that respect business time, not machine time

Rule 81Loading State Dignity

Never show spinners for <300ms operations—use optimistic UI instead. For operations 300ms-3s, show subtle progress indicator with no text. For >3s operations, show progress with context: 'Processing 47 of 200 records' or 'Encrypting document (12%)'. For background tasks, use minimized progress bar at top. Always allow user to continue working—never block entire interface unless absolutely necessary. Failed operations follow Rule 38 (Zero Displacement) for error display.

Article
III · Visible State
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Generic 'Please wait...' or 'Loading...' messages; Spinners for operations under 300ms; No indication of progress for long operations; Blocking entire UI for background tasks
Why
Waiting with information is patience; waiting without it is anxiety.
Rule 91Business Time

Interfaces respect business time, not machine time. After a critical action, the result stays long enough to be registered; periods, cutoffs, and deadlines are shown in operational terms; long operations acknowledge the wait.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Instant resets after critical actions; Machine-speed transitions the eye cannot follow; Timeouts that ignore operational reality
Why
Machines reset instantly; humans need a moment to vibe what just happened.

Set 29 · Declaration Governance

The law reaches the declaration layer: what the declaration checker enforces about norms, flows, and authority. These articles existed in the corpus (as Rules 84 and 88 of an earlier numbering) and were already cited by the linter; this set canonizes them into the constitution of record.

Rule 82Perceivable State

If the system knows something important, the operator must be able to perceive it -- in the medium the surface declares. On a screen that means visible. In an auditory or voice surface it means announced and re-requestable, because a rendering that does not persist has been made missable rather than reachable. Every norm carries a MESSAGE a human operator can read; every validation that refuses says why in plain words. Imperceivable state is a violation -- in the UI and in the declaration alike. An outstanding obligation is state of exactly this kind: on a summary surface every row says what it requires of the operator, or says plainly that it requires nothing. An obligation the operator must deduce from a number has been made missable rather than perceivable.

Article
III · Visible State
Tier
machine
Avoid
Norms that fail without telling the operator why; Error codes where human language belongs; Active filters, pending drafts, or permission constraints the user cannot see; Background operations with no visible trace
Why
A user who reasons from state they cannot perceive has been harmed by the interface.
Rule 83Predictable Authority

No control may change meaning based on hidden context: same action, same consequence; same icon, same intent. In declarations, every step that commits to [the estate's store] names its ACTOR, and every role a target claims is declared in governance. Ambiguity is operational risk.

Article
V · Predictable Authority
Tier
machine
Avoid
Irreversible commits with no declared actor; Targets claiming roles that governance never declared; Controls that change meaning based on hidden context; Role differences left implicit
Why
Ambiguous authority is operational risk; sameness of meaning is how trust scales.
Rule 126Foreign Data Says It Is Foreign

Data the application does not own must be visibly marked wherever it appears — in a table, a card, a field, a report. Without clicking, hovering or asking, an operator must be able to tell which values are governed records the application is accountable for, and which are a window onto a system it merely reads. The marker is consistent across the application and survives both vibes, and it names the source where the source changes the meaning. Freshness travels with it: referenced data carries when it was read, because a window onto a system that is currently unreachable is showing the past.

Article
III · Visible State
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Referenced rows rendered exactly like governed records; A screen where the operator cannot tell what the application owns from what it borrows; Provenance available only by hovering, clicking through, or opening a detail panel; A value read from an unreachable system shown as if it were current
Why
An operator acts on what they see. A governed record carries the application's accountability — it walked a flow, an actor stands behind it, the ledger can prove it. A referenced value carries none of that and may already be stale. Presenting the two identically invites a decision taken on the wrong footing, and the operator will never know they took it.
Rule 130Every Element Serves an Intent

Every element of an interface traces to at least one declared intent: the verb the user is performing when they meet it. An element that traces to none is removed, or the intent it was always meant to serve is declared, and declaring it is the moment the element is first asked what it is for. The trace is made in the declaration and not in the look of the element, so it holds in every medium: a printed figure, a spoken status and a control each answer to the intent they carry.

Article
II · Intent Over Mechanics
Tier
machine
Avoid
An element that is there because a template, a framework or a predecessor put it there, and that no intent of the user, a person or an agent, asks for; An indicator or a control that no declaration traces to a verb the user is performing; Keeping an element in case someone needs it, with no intent that would reach for it; Decoration that takes the shape of information or of a choice
Why
An element no intent asks for competes with the ones that matter (Article I) and answers a question nobody put. The person spends attention deciding it is irrelevant, or takes it for a choice. Being able to name the intent is the cheapest test an element has to pass, and an element that cannot pass it is mechanics, which Article II puts below intent.

Set 30 · The Field Vibe

Law forged at 375 pixels: the kitchen campaign [of a product of the estate] distilled. These rules govern the field/touch vibe — each was paid for by a real failure before it was written.

Rule 90One Action Per Screen

Every screen proposes one clear next action -- a "what now?" the operator can seize in three seconds. Details exist behind intent, not in front of it. If the primary action is not obvious at a glance, the screen failed.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
machine-later
Avoid
Screens requiring study before use; Dashboards that answer questions nobody asked; All data visible because it exists
Why
A screen with one clear action can be used at a glance, under pressure, in a kitchen.
Rule 92A Sheet Is a Hover, Not a Navigation

A sheet or popup hovers over the place the user stands; it never navigates. Closing returns exactly where they were -- same scroll, same context. The backdrop freezes the world; the sheet rises from the bottom, within thumb reach.

Article
II · Intent Over Mechanics
Tier
machine-later
Avoid
Overlays that navigate away from the page; Sheets that lose the scroll position on close; Backdrops that scroll the page beneath
Why
An overlay that navigates steals the place the user trusted it to keep.
Rule 93Navigation Invariance and the Sacred Back

Primary navigation keeps its position on every screen of a vibe. The hardware or browser back is an intent: intercept it, honor it, and never let the app close by surprise. Every screen opens from the top.

Article
IV · Reversibility
Tier
machine-later
Avoid
Navigation that moves or reflows across screens; Hardware back closing the app mid-task; Back paths that skip or reorder history
Why
The app must never close by surprise; the hardware back is an intent, not an accident.
Rule 95Zero Horizontal Scroll

The horizontal axis is forbidden to hide data in the field vibe. Lists are flex rows: amounts and dates unbreakable, names truncate with ellipsis. If a table cannot fit, it is not a table here -- it is a list wearing the wrong clothes. This rule is field-vibe law and does not reach a desktop surface; Rule 129 carries the general case, and Rule 14 already forbids the overflow container everywhere.

Article
I · Calm
Tier
machine-later
Avoid
Tables forced into phone lists; Content wider than the viewport; Charts that overflow their canvas
Why
The second axis hides data on exactly the devices that can least afford it.
Rule 96Contextual Defaults

No view opens on 'everything.' Every list opens pre-filtered to the task's slice -- this week, the pending ones, this supplier -- and a contextual entry opens the exact item, not the list that contains it.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
machine-later
Avoid
Opening on 'all records'; Filters reset on every visit; Entry links that dump into unfiltered lists
Why
'Everything' is not a view; the task's slice is.

Set 31 · Intelligence Under Law

The agentic era governed: an AI is an actor under the constitution, never an authority above it. Same norms, same audit, same dignity.

Rule 97The Agent Is an Actor

An intelligent agent participating in a flow is an ACTOR: named in the step, subject to the same validations, norms, signatures, and audit trail as any human. The agent is not a ghost in the machine -- it is a citizen of the same law.

Article
V · Predictable Authority
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Agent actions outside the audit trail; Model calls that bypass norms; AI features exempted from the constitution
Why
An agent outside the law is a ghost; inside it, it is accountable like everyone else.
Rule 98Proposals, Not Commits

Intelligence advises; execution decides. A model's output is a proposal -- rendered as such, reviewable, dismissible -- and becomes a commit only through an authority the declaration names. No prompt reaches [the estate's store].

Article
V · Predictable Authority
Tier
judgment
Avoid
LLM output written directly to records; Auto-applied AI corrections; Agent-triggered irreversible operations
Why
Intelligence advises; execution decides -- the commit belongs to a named authority.
Rule 99Visible Provenance

Content produced by a model is marked as machine-made wherever it appears, and the mark travels with it. Provenance is visible state; an unmarked machine sentence is a forged signature.

Article
III · Visible State
Tier
machine-later
Avoid
AI-generated text indistinguishable from records; Suggestions styled as facts; Machine edits without attribution
Why
Machine-made content unmarked is invisible state of the most corrosive kind.
Rule 100Deterministic Islands

Business numbers are quoted from the record, never regenerated by a model. An assistant may explain a figure, link it, or put it in context -- the digits themselves come from the deterministic island, verbatim.

Article
III · Visible State
Tier
machine-later
Avoid
AI summaries that restate figures; Rounded or paraphrased amounts in explanations; Charts drawn from model output instead of records
Why
A paraphrased number is a different number; business figures are quoted, never improvised.
Rule 101The Dignity Contract

Machine-facing language never blames, shames, or compares. A refusal states the circumstance, not the failure: "current criteria were not met" carries the same fact as "you failed" -- without the insult. Every rejection offers a next step.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Messages implying user incompetence; Comparisons to other users; Service withheld as pressure
Why
Software that blames diminishes; the fact can always be stated without the insult.
Rule 102The Right to a Human

Wherever an intelligent system serves an operator or a customer, a human path is always available, clearly labeled, and free of penalty. Escalation carries the context along; nobody restarts their story.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Support mazes that end at a bot; Human contact hidden or penalized; Escalation that loses the context
Why
No machine may be the last resort; a person must be reachable without penalty.
Rule 103Grounded Proactivity

A proactive intervention fires only from a declared trigger -- a norm, a threshold, a schedule -- never from an undeclared hunch. Calm governs what the machine says, not just what it shows; silence is the assistant's default vibe.

Article
I · Calm
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Assistants that interrupt on model whim; Unsolicited suggestions during focused work; Proactive notifications without declared triggers
Why
An assistant that interrupts on a hunch spends attention it did not earn.
Rule 104Machine Legibility

The interface is legible to machines for the same reason it is legible to screen readers: semantic structure, durable named anchors, declared intents. Accessibility law, agent-interop law and multi-modal law are one body of law with three beneficiaries.

Article
II · Intent Over Mechanics
Tier
machine-later
Avoid
Meaning conveyed only by pixels; Anchors on DOM order or coordinates; Interfaces agents must scrape to read
Why
What a screen reader can operate, an agent can operate and a non-visual medium can render; legibility is one law with three beneficiaries.
Rule 121The Assistant Never Masks the Work

The agent's calling surface is the one floating affordance an interface may carry, and it earns that exception by being minimal: a small circle with a mark, its name appearing only on hover, its expanded surface never covering the work the operator is deciding about. The assistant is a colleague at the elbow, not a billboard over the desk. Rule 110 keeps everything else out of the air; this rule disciplines the one thing allowed to float.

Article
VI · Operator Primacy and Vibes
Tier
judgment
Avoid
A floating agent widget with a permanent label eating screen width; An assistant panel that covers the content the operator is acting on; An agent affordance that cannot be dismissed or moved off the work
Why
An assistant that hides the work it is meant to help with has inverted its own purpose.
Rule 124The Generator Ships a Working Thing

A generator -- human-driven or AI -- ships artifacts that work the moment they are opened: real sample data derived from the declarations, typed inputs introspected from the entities, a simulator when the target cannot run in place, and an embedded, didactic account of what was generated, why, and how to regenerate it differently. Scaffolding is a promise, not a deliverable; the operator should never have to finish the machine's work to evaluate it.

Article
II · Intent Over Mechanics
Tier
judgment
Avoid
Scaffolding presented as a result; Empty tables and placeholder fields where sample data belongs; A generated app the user must finish before they can judge it; Output with no account of what was generated, why, and how to change it
Why
An empty shell teaches nothing and proves less. The generated thing is the argument for the generator -- it must stand up on its own.

Appendix C

The forty diagnostics

Draft

Printed at build on 2026-11-25 01:37 UTC+01:00 from the files of Zayn at release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), and from the book's own registers.

This appendix lists the 40 kinds of finding of the verifier's contract, by level: the code, the severity, the contract's own sentence, and what the contract binds the code to in the law. An error is a refusal; a warning is a finding that lets the declaration pass. Chapter 9 gives the four levels.

CodeLevel and severityThe contract's sentenceWhat it cites
UNKNOWN_INTENT1, errorA verb in SATISFIES or ALWAYS_REACHABLE is not one of the 22.Article II
UNSPECIFIED_DECLARATION1, warningA .zayn declaration kind outside the ten this language defines (WIDGET, USER).Article II
DUPLICATE_FIELD1, errorA field key appears more than once in one declaration.nothing
DUPLICATE_DECLARATION1, errorTwo declarations share a kind and a name.nothing
UNKNOWN_SIGNAL1, errorA value in SIGNALS is not one of Rule 118's five semantic statuses.Rule 118; Article I
UNKNOWN_ROLE1, errorA ROLE value is not one of the five promises this language defines.Article II
UNKNOWN_FIELD1, errorA field name is not one the grammar defines in the form it is written.nothing
SYNTAX_ERROR1, errorThe source does not parse as DEFINE <KIND> <name> ( field, ... ).nothing
UNEXPECTED_CHARACTER1, errorThe source holds a character the lexer has no token for.nothing
UNTERMINATED_STRING1, errorA string is opened and the file ends before it closes.nothing
SELECT_ACT_COLLAPSE2, errorSelection has become execution: SATISFIES holds SELECT and ACT without CONFIRM.Rule 16; Article II
READ_ACT_COLLAPSE2, errorA reading surface mutates: SATISFIES holds READ and ACT.Rule 16; Article II
MISSING_UNDO2, errorAn act declares no way back: SATISFIES holds ACT, ALWAYS_REACHABLE lacks UNDO.Rule 79; Article IV; The Right to Reverse
MISSING_CANCEL2, errorA flow that acts cannot be abandoned: ALWAYS_REACHABLE lacks CANCEL.Rule 26; Article IV; The Right to Leave
TRAPPED_FLOW2, errorA multi-step flow has no reachable EXIT.Rule 51, Rule 53; Article II; The Right to Leave
DECORATIVE_ANIMATION2, errorMotion or feedback that reports no state.Rule 112; Article I
INTENT_FLOW_NO_SATISFIES2, warningAn INTENT_FLOW declares no intents.Article II
INVALID_PERSPECTIVE2, errorPERSPECTIVE outside its enumeration.nothing
INVALID_TONE2, errorTONE outside its enumeration.nothing
UNRESOLVED_INTENT_FLOW2, warningAn INTENT_FLOW reference names no declared flow.nothing
VIBE_STRIPS_RIGHT2, errorA VIBE suppresses an intent another declaration guarantees as ALWAYS_REACHABLE.Article VI
UNKNOWN_MEDIUM2, errorSURFACE_AS names a medium outside the ten this language defines.nothing
VERB_NOT_CARRIED2, errorA declaration satisfies, or promises to keep reachable, an intent the declared medium cannot carry at all.Rule 82; Article II
EXPRESSION_ORPHAN2, errorAn expression field is declared on a declaration that satisfies no intent.Article II
SIGNAL_UNPERCEIVABLE2, errorEvery semantic status a surface declares renders as absence in the medium it declared.Rule 82; Article III; The Right to Know
ROLE_MISPLACED2, errorROLE is declared on a kind that is not an INTERACTION.Article II
ROLE_ACTS_WITHOUT_CONSEQUENCE2, errorA control promising to change nothing declares that it acts.Rule 119, Rule 112, Rule 16; Article II
ROLE_PROMISE_BROKEN2, errorA reversible control keeps no reachable UNDO.Rule 79; Article IV; The Right to Reverse
IRREVERSIBLE_CLAIMS_UNDO2, errorAn irreversible control declares an UNDO it cannot honour.Rule 79; Article IV; The Right to Reverse
PROPOSAL_COMMITS2, errorA proposal acts without naming the authority that accepted it.Rule 98, Rule 83; Article V
ROLE_UNDECLARED2, warningA surface declares interactions and gives none of them a role.nothing
FIELD_MISPLACED2, errorA field is declared on a kind that does not declare it.Article II
MENU_LABEL_REPEATS_PARENT2, errorA menu entry's label repeats the label of the entry it sits under.Rule 116; Article III
MENU_LANDING_NOT_FIRST2, errorA section with children does not list its landing surface first among them.Rule 116; Article III
MENU_LABEL_DUPLICATE2, errorTwo entries at one level of a menu share a label.Rule 116; Article III
INTENT_ORPHAN3, errorA declared element traces to no intent.Rule 130; Article II
INVISIBLE_STATE3, errorThe system holds state the operator must know, and no surface declares showing it.Rule 82; Article III; The Right to Know
HIDDEN_AUTHORITY3, errorA consequential act names no actor.Rule 83; Article V
UNRESOLVED_ENTITY3, warningA VISIBLE_ENTITIES name resolves to no entity in the model.nothing
LAYOUT_DISPLACEMENT4, errorArriving content reserves no space and shoves the reading when it lands.Rule 38; Article I; The Right to Act Without Fear
